name: Northwest Corner (Boving-Pollack Route)
approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of Hwy 20 (elev. ~5,400 ft), about one mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook and roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop. Follow the well-graded Blue Lake Trail southwest through subalpine forest. At about 1.4-1.5 miles, watch for a signed junction: the main trail continues straight toward Blue Lake, while a climber's path splits left/south, signed for "Liberty Bell Trail #727 – Climbing Access," reached just past a small stream/meadow that is the last reliable water source before the basin. Take the climber's trail, which switchbacks up through slabs, talus, and heather meadows into the Liberty Bell/Early Winters basin beneath the west faces of the spire group — roughly another 0.5 mile and 1,000-1,300 ft of gain, putting total approach distance at about 2 miles with 1,300-1,600 ft of gain from the car (most parties report 1-2 hours). From the upper basin, continue scrambling/traversing north along the base of North Early Winters Spire's west side to a distinctive corner/crack system that leads to a tree-covered ledge — the shared start for the Northwest Corner and West Face. Hazards: lingering snow and occasional avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully well into June (many early-season parties boot or ski the lower approach), talus and slab sections with some route-finding among braided climbers' paths, and no dependable water once past the stream near the Liberty Bell Trail junction, so fill up there.
descent:
Two established ways off the summit; both are widely used and either works, but they return you to different spots relative to a gear stash at the base.

Bolted West Face rappel line (most direct back to packs at the base of NW Corner/West Face): from the summit, downclimb/walk skier's-left to the top of a clean, purpose-bolted rappel line down the right side of the West Face. Six bolted (2-bolt) rappel stations in a nearly direct line bring you back down to essentially the same spot where you left your pack at the base of the route. Pulls are reported as clean and the line is efficient — regulars find it a breeze. A single 60m rope is just barely sufficient (one station, reportedly the 3rd rappel, is tight enough that you may need to reach down to clip your PAS/daisy to the anchor and feed rope through your device to reach it); a 70m rope removes that squeeze and is the more comfortable choice. No natural anchors needed on this line — it's fully bolted.

Classic notch/chockstone descent (South/Southwest Gully): downclimb and rappel the south side into the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then continue down the Southwest Gully (the South Early Winter Spire "Chockstone Route" descent). This runs three single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the notch/gully (which often holds snow even in summer), followed by one spectacular, largely free-hanging double-rope rappel down and past a huge chockstone (~50 ft of air), then a final short rappel (~30 ft, off a tree anchor) or downclimb/scramble to reach the base. Total is about 4-5 rappels on this line. Anchors are natural/fixed slings around the chockstone and trees rather than bolts — inspect webbing before trusting it. Summit-to-base time on this descent is typically around 1.5-2 hours. This option is the standard descent if you climbed a route on the south/southwest side, or as a backup if the West Face bolt line is congested or iced.
hazards: The route includes wide flake and offwidth pitches that require big gear; running low on large cams is a real risk.
Long, sometimes traversing pitches create rope drag that must be managed with long runners.

The Early Winters Spires are a serious alpine setting: on May 10, 2025, three climbers died and a fourth was seriously injured when a single old, rusted piton anchor pulled out while multiple people were clipped to it and rappelling in the Early Winter Couloir, the gully separating North and South Early Winters Spire (a different line than this route's own NW Corner descent gully). It's a hard reminder never to trust an old fixed pin without backup and never to load one anchor point with an entire party.

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail, then north along the base of the west side
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Nearly all the routes on North Early Winters Spire are on its west side, so the Blue Lake Trailhead is the right side of the mountain to start from — the hairpin pullout on the east serves the East Buttress and couloir lines, not this one.

From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about a mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail for roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction, which sits just past a small stream and is marked with a large cairn. That stream is your last reliable water.

Trail #727 switchbacks up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces. Approach as if for South Early Winters Spire and then traverse left (north) along the base of the formations, scrambling, until you are under North Early Winters Spire. Most parties report one to two hours from the car.
hazards: lingering snow and avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully into June
braided climbers' paths through the upper talus make it easy to drift onto the wrong formation
no water past the stream at the Trail #727 junction
poorly protected chimney section low on the first pitch

name: North Face
approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead, a small pullout on SR-20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the main, well-graded Blue Lake Trail through forest for about 1.5 to 2 miles. Watch for a cairned, well-worn climbers' boot path splitting off uphill to the left toward the Liberty Bell group cirque — this junction is easy to miss if you're not watching for it. From the split, the climbers' path steepens considerably, switchbacking up talus and heather benches beneath Concord and Lexington Towers. Budget roughly 1.5-2 hours and about 1,900-2,000 ft of gain from the trailhead to reach the Concord-Lexington col (the notch between the two towers), which is the start of the North Face route. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin can provide water in early season but are unreliable by mid-to-late summer — carry water from the trailhead. Lingering snow/firm névé in the upper gully approaching the col is common into early summer and may warrant an axe or traction.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the exposed 'Stegosaur' ridge crest pitch (3rd/low-5th class scrambling along a knobby, horn-studded ridge) back down to the notch just below the summit block — most parties downclimb this rather than rappel it. From that notch, make two single-rope rappels (each is about 30m, so a single 60m rope reaches) down the north face back to the Concord-Lexington col; documented descents used natural gear anchors — slings around horns — rather than fixed bolts or chains, so bring extra webbing/cord to back up or replace tat. Total time from summit to the col is about 20 minutes for a competent party. From the col, reverse the approach: descend the talus/heather gully back to the Blue Lake climbers' path and follow it back to the Blue Lake Trail and trailhead. Many parties link this route with a Concord Tower climb, rappelling from Concord's summit into the shared col before starting Lexington's North Face, so plan rope/anchor needs accordingly if doing a link-up.
hazards: loose blocky rock on both the approach talus and the lower two pitches
exposed 4th/low-5th-class ridge traverse on the summit pitch ('the Stegosaur')
rappel anchors are unfixed slung horns — inspect slings before weighting them

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Concord-Lexington gully
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 just under a mile west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail until the terrain opens up — around a mile and a half to two miles — and pick up the well-established climbers' path branching left at a large cairn.

From there, leave the line most parties take toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and work up into the next gully south, the one that separates Lexington Tower from Concord Tower. As you gain height in that gully a decent boot path shows up along its left side; use it. It brings you to the Concord-Lexington col.

Carry water from the trailhead. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin dry up by mid-summer.
hazards: loose rock in the Concord-Lexington gully
lingering firm snow or névé in the upper gully into early summer — axe or traction useful
the descent uses slung horns rather than fixed anchors, so carry spare webbing

waysIn.name: Early-season snow to the Concord-Lexington col
waysIn.season: Highway opening through late Jun
waysIn.notes:
Same approach, but the upper gully to the col commonly holds firm snow into early summer, which buries the boot path along its left side and turns the last stretch into a snow climb. Carry an axe, and crampons if it is refrozen.

SR-20 is gated across Washington Pass through the winter — typically closing in late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May — so there is no drive-up access until the highway reopens.
hazards: firm snow in the gully below the col
moat where snow meets the Lexington wall
SR-20 closed in winter — no vehicle access until reopening
waysIn.whyThisWay: Early season, from when the highway opens until late June, while the gully to the col still holds firm snow that buries the boot path; bring an axe, and crampons if it is refrozen.

name: Fight or Flight
approach: Two approaches exist, both multi-day. The first-ascent party came from Canada: from Lightning Lake in E.C. Manning Provincial Park, about seven miles of trail over the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then cross-country south over the border, through the Princess Creek basin and into the Crow Creek drainage below Castle's north face to the toe of the north-face glacier. Walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, so that line is recorded, not recommended. The lawful approach is from the US side: boat or hike up Ross Lake from the WA-20/Ross Dam trailhead (permit from the North Cascades Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount) to Lightning Creek, then follow the Lightning Creek Trail and the abandoned, increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek Trail past the Freezeout cabin (3,600 ft), a much longer multi-day trudge. Both approaches finish by crossing the mellow north-face glacier to the base of the buttress -- watch for an awkward bergschrund/moat at the start of the route.
descent: From the top of the route, descend via Castle Peak's east ridge to an obvious col, then down a snow finger back toward the approach glacier/basin, rather than reversing the climbing line.
hazards: remote, glacier-crossing approach
proximity to the US/Canada border on the Canada-side approach — legal/permit considerations
long multi-pitch commitment with descent only via the east ridge, not a reversal of the route

waysIn.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
waysIn.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
waysIn.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
hazards: Boat crossing of Ross Lake needed; a long multi-day approach with a retreat measured in days
Abandoned, brushy Freezeout Creek trail; tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft
Steep rock-and-alder diagonal above the trail junction is the hardest navigation of the walk
Awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face
Several unmarked lines on one wall; descent by the east ridge and snow finger, not the route reversed

waysIn.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
waysIn.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
waysIn.notes:
Read the legal point first. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it follows the marked trail from Lightning Lake up the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south over the boundary, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country, which is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face
Several unmarked lines on one wall; descent by the east ridge and snow finger, not the route reversed
Very remote, multi-day approach with no quick rescue
waysIn.whyThisWay: Walks in from the Canadian provincial park over Frosty Mountain, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

waysIn.name: Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass
waysIn.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.
hazards: Very long high walk of about 27 miles, a 3-5 day trip with no shortcut
Harts Pass road is single lane, steep and exposed; usually opens only in July; wildfire can close it
Snow lingering on north-facing traverses into August; sparse water along the crest
Wind and cold on the open crest, far from the car if weather turns
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall, worse once sun hits the face; descent by the east ridge and snow finger
waysIn.whyThisWay: When no boat is available and you want to stay in the United States; it is about 27 miles each way along the crest from Harts Pass, which usually opens only in July.

name: Southwest Slopes / South Ridge
approach: From the Wolf Creek Trailhead (~2,950 ft, end of FS Road 5005 west of Winthrop) follow Wolf Creek Trail #527 roughly 10 miles up the Wolf Creek valley to Gardner Meadows, then continue off-trail north into Wolf Creek Basin (typical high camp ~6,200-6,400 ft) below the Gardner/North Gardner saddle. A long, multi-day approach for most parties (roughly 27 miles round trip with ~7,300 ft of gain for the full trip).
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — there is no rappelling on this route. From the summit, retrace the south ridge/traverse back to Point 8,487, staying on the Class 1-2 line along or just below the crest (contour under the ridge horns rather than staying strictly on the crest). From Point 8,487, drop back into the upper basin: parties commonly plunge-step down scree, glissade remaining snow, and finish on grass back down to the Wolf Creek Basin camp/contour line (roughly 1-1.5 hrs from summit to camp for a fit party in good conditions). From the basin, reverse the off-trail contour back to Gardner Meadows and rejoin Wolf Creek Trail #527 for the long hike out to the trailhead. This is a full walk-off/downclimb — no technical rappels are involved anywhere on this route; the only technical hazard is loose scree/talus and any lingering snow on the ridge approach slopes.
hazards: routefinding on broad slopes and along the south ridge
afternoon thunderstorms
blowdown and fire-damaged snags along the lower Wolf Creek Trail

waysIn.name: Wolf Creek Trail to Gardner Meadows
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September; snow into July
waysIn.notes: About ten miles of valley trail up Wolf Creek from the road end west of Winthrop gets you to Gardner Meadows, and that is where the walking ends and the day begins. Most parties camp in the meadows or carry on to a high bivy in Wolf Creek Basin and take the summit the next morning, often adding the slightly lower neighbouring summit from the same camp. The lower trail runs through burned forest with heavy blowdown, little shade and standing dead snags, so pick a camp clear of them and expect a hot, dusty walk in late summer. Fill water in the creek at the meadows — sources above are unreliable to absent, and the scree slopes offer none at all.
hazards: About 1,400 ft of loose scree below the false summit, tedious up and worse down
Route-finding on broad featureless slopes and around cliff bands, with no cairned line
Fire-killed snags that shed limbs and topple in wind, at the meadows and along the lower trail
No reliable water above the meadows
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter on the high ridges
Lingering snow in the basin and summit bowl needing an ice axe well into early summer

name: North Ridge
approach: Two long approaches reach Whatcom Pass (~5,200 ft), and both are roughly comparable in mileage (~16-17 miles one-way). From the west: start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of Hannegan Pass Rd/FS-32, ~3,100 ft) and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles/2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass (~5,050-5,100 ft), then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley. Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail (unmaintained and rough in sections, with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris) past Copper Creek Camp and US Cabin Camp, cross the Chilliwack River by the hand-operated cable car just beyond US Cabin (or ford it), then turn up the Brush Creek Trail at its junction near mile 12 and climb past Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass — a long day or more typically split over 2 days with a valley-bottom camp. From the east: hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort (near Diablo, off SR 20) to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead (~1,600 ft) on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley — passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles — before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass. Whichever way you arrive, from Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads directly south, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge; the path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and route-finding means staying on the crest rather than following any marked line.
descent: This is a scramble route with no rappelling — a walk-off/downclimb via either the same ridge or a loop over the summit. Reversing the North Ridge directly is unpleasant: it's a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd-to-low-4th-class terrain in its final several hundred feet below the summit, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it's shorter. Many parties instead descend via the South Spur side: continue over/near the summit and down the south ridge's exposed Class 3 crest to the south-facing snowfield, glissade or plunge-step down to Perfect Pass, then loop back to Whatcom Pass either via the low-orbit traverse around the peak's east side or by crossing the Whatcom Glacier when it's consolidated (treat as glacier travel — rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season). This adds distance but trades loose downclimbing for straightforward snow. No fixed rappel anchors exist on the North Ridge itself, and rope use beyond an optional running belay on the chossiest step is not described; rappels = 0, though a party uncomfortable downclimbing the loose upper ridge could improvise a natural (rock horn/gear) anchor for a short rappel.
hazards: Loose rock on the final ~400 ft below the summit
Ridge-crest exposure, especially off the easiest 3rd-class line
Lingering snow/ice on the ridge into midsummer
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage and no easy bail

Route passes near Whatcom Glacier, reported down to bare ice with a shallow crevasse crossing by late August (2017 NPS climbing ranger account) — the adjacent Challenger Glacier, crossed separately from Perfect Pass, had crevasses described as open but easy to navigate on that same trip.

waysIn.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp and US Cabin Camp, cross the Chilliwack by the hand-operated cable car just beyond US Cabin (or ford it), then turn up the Brush Creek Trail at its junction near mile 12 and climb past Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.
hazards: Unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris
Chilliwack River crossing by hand-operated cable car or a ford
Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Downclimbing that ground with an overnight pack is the riskier option
Lingering snow and ice on the ridge into midsummer
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage and no easy bail
No fixed anchors anywhere on the ridge

waysIn.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.
hazards: A 16-mile valley walk that depends on a water-taxi booking at both ends
Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Returning over the summit strands you on the wrong side of the peak from this trailhead
Lingering snow and ice on the ridge into midsummer
Long, remote approach with no cell coverage and no easy bail
Whatcom Glacier loop back to the pass needs glacier travel gear
waysIn.whyThisWay: When starting from the SR-20 side or linking a Pickets traverse out to Ross Lake; it skips the long Hannegan drive but needs a water taxi booked ahead from the resort.

name: North Ridge
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different stop from the Eldorado trailhead about 2.5 miles down-road, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.
descent: From tower summit, establish anchor and rappel 40 feet. Reverse fourth-class scrambling pitches and traverse back toward notch before descending to camp.
hazards: Rockfall from ridge and tower is primary hazard
Inclement weather strikes rapidly; afternoon thunderstorms common
Short tower summit presents exposure; most parties turn around before absolute top

waysIn.name: Boston Basin toward the Cat Scratch gullies, then the notch right of the ridge
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep; July and August are the most settled, and snow can linger around camp into July
waysIn.notes:
The Aiguille is a small formation, not a peak of its own: it is the cockscomb dividing the high Forbidden basin from Torment basin, with the Taboo Glacier on its west side and an unnamed glacier on its east, sitting just south of the Torment-Forbidden traverse line. It is named for its resemblance to the Chamonix aiguille of the same shape — a deliberate echo, and a coincidence worth being clear about rather than a mistake.

Approach exactly as for Forbidden Peak: Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles to the small pullout near 3,200 ft opposite Johannesburg, the old Diamond Mine roadbed, then the steep unmaintained climbers' path with several stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the Boston Basin camps at about 5,300 and 6,400 ft.

From camp, head up toward the Forbidden Gully / Cat Scratch gullies area and traverse to the notch. It is a half-day objective from camp, which is most of its appeal.
hazards: Rockfall off the ridge and the tower is the primary hazard
Weather that builds fast, with afternoon thunderstorms usual
A very small, exposed tower top that many parties choose not to stand on
Approach terrain shared with Forbidden's West Ridge descent, so parties may be above you in the gullies

name: West Ridge
approach: Via Mosquito Lake Road (off SR 542 east of Deming) to a bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38; park at the gate and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads (commonly covered by mountain bike) to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.
descent: Reverse the West Ridge to the approach; the friction rock makes downclimbing straightforward. In early season (roughly late May into mid-July), many parties instead glissade a long, steep snowfield on the north slope and traverse back to rejoin the West Ridge trail near 4,600 ft.
hazards: Sustained 3rd/4th-class exposure on the ridge crest, worse if you drift off the 'stay left' line
Complex, unmarked logging-road network - wrong turns at the forks add significant miles
Wet brush and alder on the clearcut sections can soak clothing and packs in any damp weather
Steep snow on the north-face descent option requires an axe (and crampons if firm) - a fall here would be a long slide
Loose rock/scree on the north face once snow cover melts out
Unpredictable gate closures on a private-land approach - this is not maintained Forest Service trail
Minimal to no cell coverage on most of the route

name: Northwest Arete
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of Icicle Creek Road/FR-7600 near Leavenworth), follow the Stuart Lake Trail; at roughly 45 minutes in, stay straight/right past the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction rather than turning off. Continue on the Stuart Lake Trail until you can reasonably leave it and go cross-country toward Mountaineer Creek — parties describe picking up a faint boot path here before it fades. From there it's sustained off-trail travel: schwack up through a boulder field, cross talus, and work past slabs near a waterfall before a final steeper push into the open basin at the base of Argonaut's north/northwest side (roughly 4 hours car-to-basin for a fit, efficient party). Above the basin, climb a snow finger (can be firm/icy and intimidating late in the season — carry an axe and consider crampons) up to the Northwest Buttress, then follow it to the top of a connecting gully and a small col — this is the start of the roped climbing, 6-7 pitches of generally solid, blocky Class 4 to 5.6 rock with mostly straightforward route-finding. Hazards: the Mountaineer Creek drainage is notorious for dense slide alder and brush lower down (stay on talus to climber's-right where possible to avoid the worst of it), wet/mossy log crossings over the creek, and a real chance of losing the boot path in the boulder field — expect route-finding by feel rather than a marked trail for most of this approach. Note that permits/quota rules apply to camping on the north side of Stuart Ridge in this basin if you're not doing it car-to-car.
descent: Do not expect to simply reverse the arete pitch-for-pitch — the standard descent traverses off to the east side of the mountain and down to the Argonaut-Colchuck col, and it typically takes about 4 rappels: from near the top of the route, a rappel (a single 60 m rope reaches) down the upper northeast-face snowfield; a short scramble to a tree anchor for the next rappel down more broken, more reasonable terrain (staying skier's-left / closer to the Northeast Ridge tends to find better anchors and avoid rope-snag terrain); a short scramble through a notch onto the East Face; then two further rappels down the East Face to its base. Anchors are a mix of natural options (trees, slung blocks/horns) and whatever fixed tat previous parties have left — there is no bolted rappel line here, so carry extra webbing/cord and be prepared to build an anchor if you can't find one. From the base of the East Face, descend scree, snow, and talus back down toward the approach basin/waterfall slabs, then reverse the long cross-country approach back to the Stuart Lake Trail and out. Route-finding on this descent is genuinely tricky — parties describe real uncertainty about the best line down, confusing terrain, and rope-snag concerns, so this is not a descent to rush or attempt in poor visibility.
hazards: loose rock and dirty terrain on the upper pitches
a steep, sometimes icy 40+ degree couloir on the approach
wet rock and moss low on the route
dense brush on the Mountaineer Creek approach
afternoon thunderstorms and fast-changing weather
mosquitoes in the approach basin in early/midsummer

waysIn.name: Stuart Lake TH cross-country up Mountaineer Creek to the north basin
waysIn.season: mid-Jul-Sep; parties report significant snow and slush still hampering things into late June
waysIn.notes:
From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail and go straight past the Colchuck Lake turnoff. Continue to about 4,700 ft, where a faint path leaves the trail for Mountaineer Creek. Follow it over and down to the creek, then up the creek to roughly 4,780 ft, and bushwhack up to a boulder field below Argonaut at about 4,925 ft.

Traverse the boulders following cairns south-southwest and cut through slide alder — this brush is the notorious part of the day, and staying on talus to climber's right where you can avoids the worst of it. Then head up in or beside the trees, through boulders, talus, scree and dry creek beds, past waterfall slabs, into the north basin below Argonaut at about 6,700 ft. Roughly four hours car-to-basin for an efficient party.

Expect to lose the boot path in the boulder field. Most of this approach is navigated by feel; there is no marked trail. Wet, mossy logs over Mountaineer Creek are a nuisance in both directions.
hazards: Dense slide alder in the Mountaineer Creek drainage
Wet, mossy log crossings of Mountaineer Creek
Boot path disappears in the boulder field — sustained off-trail navigation
Firm or icy snow finger to the col late season
Waterfall slabs on the approach
Descent route-finding is genuinely tricky and is not a place to be in poor visibility

name: Northwest Buttress
approach: Same Bedal Creek approach as Sloan's other West Face routes. From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096 to the Bedal Creek Trailhead (~2,790 ft) and follow Bedal Creek Trail #705 along the creek through old growth until the maintained tread ends at a washout below the West Face basin (roughly 1.5–2.5 miles in). Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto a climber's path that climbs steeply through forest from about 3,500 ft to 4,900 ft, then crosses talus and a meadow bench to the 5,300 ft saddle between Bedal Peak and Sloan Peak (last water here or at nearby cascading streams). From the meadows below the broad West Face, the Northwest Buttress route begins on a corner of darker rock at the lowest, leftmost part of the face — no glacier travel is needed to reach the start, unlike the standard Corkscrew line, which continues past this point onto the ice. Expect brush and route-finding in the forest band; best conditions are mid-to-late season (July–September) once snowmelt clears the lower approach.
descent: The route tops out via a short hand crack onto the upper mountain, then 3rd/4th class scrambling to a sub-summit and the main summit, joining the upper Corkscrew line. From there, descent follows the same terrain used by parties finishing the Southwest Face routes: down the SE Shelf/Corkscrew ledge system. This involves one roped pitch of low 5th-class downclimbing to gain the main ledge system, then one rappel off the end of the SE Shelf back down to the glacier snowfield; parties descending closer to the true summit sometimes need an additional rappel off a ledge system roughly 400–500 ft below the top before joining that shelf. Once back on the glacier, rope up for crevasse hazard, cross to the 5,800 ft saddle on the ridge above it, drop to the 5,300 ft Bedal-Sloan saddle, and reverse the approach back through the meadow, forest, and washout to the trailhead.
hazards: Loose/rotten rock exists off-route on the north-face traverse below the crux.
Late-season snowmelt can complicate the approach and lower buttress.

waysIn.name: Bedal Creek to the West Face meadows
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft; Bedal Creek Trail #705 along the creek through old growth until the maintained tread gives out at a washout below the West Face basin, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in.

Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves left near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft and is usually flagged pink — then climb steeply through forest to about 4,900 ft, cross talus and a meadow bench, and reach the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft. Water here or at the streams just below.

From the saddle stay in the meadows below the broad West Face. Do not continue southeast toward the glacier toe.
hazards: Brushy, blowdown-choked washout where the maintained trail ends
Route-finding through the forest band above the washout
Loose rock in the meadow-to-face transition

name: Northwest Face
approach: The Temple (Kangaroo Temple, on Kangaroo Ridge) is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass — the same parking area used for the neighboring Hairpin Crags/Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus (faint, intermittently cairned) up to Kangaroo Pass, about 1 hour. From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face, or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. Expect about 11 hours car to car. For this specific route: boulder field to Kangaroo Pass, traverse left to the gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger, then ascend toward the notch. Northwest Face breaks off onto a climber's trail about 200 ft below the notch instead of continuing into the boulder-choked gully.
descent: From the summit, downclimb or scramble to the fixed rappel anchors on the north side of the formation. Accounts differ slightly — some parties do two full-length 30 m rappels, others do three shorter single-rope rappels (roughly 150-160+ ft total) to avoid rope-stuck issues — landing at or near the North Ridge notch. From the notch, continue the standard descent gully back down to Kangaroo Pass and retrace the approach trail to the trailhead.
hazards: Runout, R-rated protection on pitches 1 and 3.
Water-streaked or wet rock on pitch 1 after snowmelt or rain.

waysIn.name: The Hairpin turnout and Kangaroo Pass, then break off the gully about 200 ft below the notch
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The Temple is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass, the same parking used for the neighbouring Hairpin Crags and Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus, faint and intermittently cairned, up to Kangaroo Pass, about an hour.

From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. Expect about 11 hours car to car.
hazards: A 200 ft window in which to leave the gully, above and below which you are on a different route
Loose talus and a boulder-choked gully
Rope-stuck issues on the descent, which is why some parties break it into three shorter rappels
Early-season snow or ice in the approach gully
No reliable water on the approach

name: Northwest Face
approach: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where FR 56 is gated, follow Dutch Miller Gap Trail 1030 — the first 7.7 miles on the closed road to Hardscrabble Horse Camp — up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley toward Dutch Miller Gap, but do not go to the gap: leave the main Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail at a small steel bridge well before Dutch Miller Gap and cut cross-country south into Summit Chief Valley; the Northwest Face is visible on the east side of that valley — a distinctly different final leg than the Northeast Face's direct ridge approach.
descent: From the summit, travel south along the ridge for several hundred feet to a small pocket glacier below the face. Cross glacier-polished slabs, trending climber's left, to regain the ridge crest at approximately 5,400'. From there, make one to two rappels down broken terrain into the valley, then traverse exposed goat ledges before a final forest descent back to the Summit Chief Valley camp. The glacier-polished slabs can be wet, snow-covered, or icy well into summer.
hazards: Loose rock on the approach talus and lower pitches.
Exposed, unprotected final ridge pitch to the summit.
Potential residual snow/ice on the pocket glacier and polished descent slabs into midsummer.

waysIn.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie, then cross-country into Summit Chief Valley
waysIn.season: August to September for the documented ascents; snow can linger in the approach gully system earlier in the summer.
waysIn.notes: Do not walk the trail to Dutch Miller Gap. From the gate at the Dingford Creek Trailhead, head up the valley on the closed road and then the trail until you reach a small steel bridge, well short of the gap — that bridge is the turnoff. Leave the trail there and travel cross-country in a southerly direction into the mouth of Summit Chief Valley, then up the valley to a camp at around the level where the timber thins. From camp the peak is on the east side of the valley: look across and up, not back at the trail.
hazards: Loose rock on the approach talus and on the lower pitches
Exposed, unprotected final ridge pitch to the summit
Residual snow and ice on the pocket glacier and the polished slabs used on the descent, into midsummer
The turnoff is a small bridge on a long valley trail with no sign — miss it and you commit to a very long day getting back

name: Northwest Ridge
approach: Reach the base via the shared Eldorado Peak approach: from the large trailhead parking area on Cascade River Road (~2,100 ft, about 20 miles from Marblemount), backtrack a short distance downstream to find a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River, then pick up the climbers' path heading east/upstream on the far bank. The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus (roughly 1,500 ft of gain) before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad basin around 5,500-5,800 ft (Roush Creek/Eldorado Basin), where scattered camps exist near 6,100 ft; most parties push on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft (roughly 5.3 mi and ~5,300 ft gain, 5-6 hours car-to-camp). From high camp, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, pass through/near the Tepeh Towers, and drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favoring its left (south) side to dodge a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season. Ascend the McAllister's steep upper apron (~30°) trending northwest to its top, below a line of gendarmes on Dorado Needle's northwest ridge crest. Watch for a moat where the glacier meets the rock — find a safe crossing point, which can deteriorate significantly by late summer — then climb a short low-5th-class pitch to gain the ridge. Crevasse hazard on both glaciers and a moat at the base are the main approach-specific concerns; carry pickets for the snow.
descent: Descend by downclimbing or rappelling the same Northwest Ridge line used on ascent. A single rappel down the final snow/rock step back to the glacier is typical, though parties sometimes downclimb this section instead if conditions allow; a 30m rope suffices for the short rock pitches, but bring a 60m single if you intend to rappel the snow pitch in one go rather than making two shorter raps. Anchors are a mix of old fixed tat on rock horns and slung natural features (horns/chockstones) rather than bolts — carry a handful of extra double-length slings and a few feet of cord/webbing to back up or replace worn anchor material, and inspect any in-situ tat carefully (one party reported an anchor block dislodging during a rappel here). The rock is fractured with loose flakes prone to catching or dislodging the rope, so manage rope stacking and pull carefully. Below the rappel, re-cross the moat (which can worsen through the season) back onto the McAllister Glacier, then reverse the approach across the McAllister and Inspiration Glaciers to high camp. An alternate snow-gully descent line exists off the ridge but is guarded by a large moat that typically still requires a short rappel to bypass, so it offers little advantage over the standard ridge descent.
hazards: crevasses on the McAllister Glacier (variable by year, generally avoidable)
large moat where the route gains the ridge
aging/degraded rappel webbing left by past parties

waysIn.name: Inspiration to McAllister, then the small col at the toe of the ridge
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September, depending on glacier and moat conditions
waysIn.notes:
Shared Eldorado approach: from the large trailhead parking area on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, about 20 miles from Marblemount, backtrack a short way downstream to a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path on the far bank. The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft, before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad basin around 5,500-5,800 ft with scattered camps near 6,100 ft. Most parties push on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — roughly 5.3 miles and 5,300 ft, five to six hours car to camp.

From high camp, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, pass through or near the Tepeh Towers saddle, and drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favouring its left (south) side to dodge a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season.

Ascend the McAllister's steep upper apron, about 30 degrees, trending northwest to its top. This is the easiest established route on the peak and is commonly used as the descent for the harder ones.
hazards: Crevasses on the McAllister Glacier, variable by year and generally avoidable
A large moat where the route gains the ridge, which deteriorates significantly by late summer
Aging and degraded rappel webbing left by past parties — one party reported an anchor block dislodging during a rappel here
Fractured rock with loose flakes prone to catching or dislodging the rope on the way down

name: Standard scramble route
approach: Mowich Lake is no longer a drive-up trailhead (see the road note): reaching it is a long walk in of its own. From the Mowich Lake trailhead, take the Spray Park Trail (the Wonderland Trail at first) about 3.5 miles to Spray Park at roughly 5,800 ft. Near 6,200 ft a way trail leaves the main trail, easy to follow for about a mile, and climbs toward the saddle between Echo Rock and Observation Rock near 7,600 ft. Stay on snow where you can to spare the meadows. The north side of Observation is steep and loose, so contour clockwise round the foot of the peak, crossing the east icefield of the Flett Glacier if it is in, to the scree and talus of the south slope, where the climb starts.
descent: Reverse the route: down the loose pumice of the south slope to the Echo-Observation saddle, then back along the way trail to Spray Park and the Spray Park Trail to Mowich Lake. Descend south and east only. Dropping west puts you on the crevassed Flett Glacier, which may be impassable late in the season. By August the snow slopes east of the summit can be icy, so carry an ice axe and crampons or microspikes, or circle well above or below them. Wear a helmet, since the rock is crumbly and anything knocked loose falls on those below.

name: West Side (LeConte Glacier)
approach: Drive Cascade River Road east from Marblemount roughly 23 miles (paved for about the first 10, then good gravel) to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,660 ft; parking area and vault toilet, North Cascades NP wilderness permit required for overnight camps). In some seasons, including 2026, the road is gated to vehicles at Eldorado (mile 20), leaving the last 3 miles to the trailhead on foot or bike. From the trailhead, follow the Cascade Pass Trail, which switchbacks about 30 times up a forested rib, gaining roughly 1,400 ft in the first 2 miles before the grade eases into a long ascending traverse through meadows, talus, and lingering snowfields to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft) at about 3.7 miles — figure 2.5-3.5 hours to the pass. This is only the start: Old Guard Peak sits deep in the Ptarmigan Mountains and is normally reached via the classic Ptarmigan Traverse, not as a day trip from the pass. From Cascade Pass, leave the maintained trail and climb south and east on a boot path/talus toward Cache Col (~6,900 ft), a rocky saddle roughly 3 hours above the pass; a steep snowfield on the col's far side (often needing an axe and crampons through midsummer) descends to Kool-Aid Lake basin (~6,320-6,800 ft), a common first camp about 6-8 miles and 2,800 ft of gain from the trailhead. From Kool-Aid Lake the route crosses a band of steep snow (pickets useful) to reach the Red Ledge, an exposed but broad Class 3 rock traverse that is the traverse's first real crux, especially if snow-covered. Beyond the ledges, follow the true-left (climber's left) edge of the Middle Cascade Glacier, roping up for crevasse hazard, staying on the less-broken upper glacier, then continue to the Spider-Formidable Col (a whiteout-prone spot where altimeter/compass/GPS route-finding matters). From the col, descend steep snow and a long sidehill traverse over snow and rock down to Yang Yang Lakes, then continue via LeConte Pass and Sentinel Pass to White Rock Lakes/the LeConte Glacier area — the standard second or third camp, roughly 12-14 hours of cumulative travel from the trailhead for parties moving efficiently. Old Guard Peak is climbed from Sentinel Pass: contour onto the LeConte Glacier and ascend a moderate, gradually-angled snow couloir/snowfinger on the peak's northwest side (watch for a bergschrund/moat late season) to gain the summit ridge, then finish on short, low-Class-3 scrambling on solid, high-friction gabbro to the true summit (8,240-8,260 ft). Water is available at Kool-Aid Lake, Yang Yang Lakes, and White Rock Lakes/tarns near the LeConte Glacier; carry a full topo map and glacier gear, as this is committing, remote glacier terrain with no easy bail once past Cache Col.
descent: Reverse the line of ascent: the short rock scramble and the Class 2-3 snow couloir back down to the LeConte Glacier, then cross the glacier to the Le Conte-Sentinel col camp. In a high-snow year a couple of very short rappels off nuts or slings may be needed on the way down, so bring a few small pieces and cord. Watch the moat and bergschrund at the foot of the couloir, and rope up for the crevassed glacier on the return to camp.
hazards: loose rock
remoteness
early-season snow

waysIn.name: Cascade Pass and the traverse corridor to the LeConte Glacier
waysIn.season: Mid-July through August is most reliable, since the route depends on the whole corridor being passable rather than on local conditions. Early trips face larger cornices at Cache Col and a more consequential Red Ledge; a low-snow autumn exposes more bare glacier ice.
waysIn.notes: This is a side trip off a multi-day high traverse, not a day climb. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and eases into a long ascending traverse through meadow and talus to the pass, where the tread ends. Leave the trail there and head south and east, traversing and climbing across the Mixup arm on boot path, talus and snow bands, then onto the Cache Glacier and up it to Cache Col; the step onto the glacier is short but steep and can be corniced, and an axe and crampons are normal here into midsummer. Descend the steep snowfield on the far side to the bench holding Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first camp. From there the Red Ledge bypasses the cliff band west of the knoll above, entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin. Past the ledge, the corridor crosses the Middle Cascade Glacier, climbs to the Spider-Formidable col and drops to the Yang Yang Lakes basin, after which a ledge system leads up onto the LeConte snowfield and glacier. Camp near the col between LeConte and Sentinel, or at White Rock Lakes, and climb the peak from there.
hazards: roped glacier travel with crevasses on the LeConte Glacier, and a bergschrund or moat at the foot of the snow ramp late season
loose rock on the upper scramble
remoteness with no easy bail once past Cache Col
steep early-season snow on the col approaches and on the ramp itself
the ramp softens to punchy postholing by afternoon, with the runout back onto the glacier

name: Northwest Ridge / PCT approach
approach: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail). When the Snowgrass Flats lot is full, park at Berry Patch Trailhead, about half a mile west along FR 2150 near Chambers Lake, where Trail 96 begins; it joins this route about 0.6 mile in, at the junction where the short hikers' path from the Snowgrass Flats lot comes in. The first stretch climbs gently through forest, crossing Goat Creek on a footbridge at about 1.9 miles. Around 2.4-2.6 miles in you'll hear and then reach the springs that form the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right - the last reliable, easy water source before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek itself; there's no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except during heavy snowmelt, when it can run fast enough to require care. Just beyond the ford (~3.9-4 miles, ~5,800 ft) the trail breaks out of forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat, a scenic rest and water-filter stop before the climb — note that camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself under Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)); parties camp instead at designated sites above/below the flats. Stay left on Trail 96 where the Bypass Trail 97 forks right toward Cispus Basin at about 3.9 miles, and continue straight past the Trail 86 junction (left, to Goat Lake) at about 4.7 miles, staying on the main track as it climbs in long benches with Mount Adams and the Goat Rocks opening up behind you. At about 5.4 miles the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 6,400 ft; turn left (north) onto the PCT. Follow the PCT north for about 1.8 miles, traversing rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill terrain on Old Snowy's west flank - snow patches can linger here into midsummer and may require an ice axe/traction for a secure traverse in early season. Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble: the last few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers. Total one-way distance is approximately 7.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain; round trip is roughly 15.5 miles, typically taking 8.5-9.5 hours car to car. After leaving US-12 the approach road is about 16 miles of unpaved washboard; no big potholes in late August, but higher clearance is more comfortable.
descent: This is a walk-off, not a technical descent - there is no rappelling on the standard northwest ridge/PCT route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 scramble off the summit block (the loose scree and blocky talus here is the descent crux - go slow, test holds, and stay alert for rock knocked loose by parties above or below you), then pick up the climbers' path back down to the PCT. From the PCT junction, follow the trail back south, again watching footing on any lingering snowfields on the exposed sidehill traverse below the ridge (these are firmest and safest to cross in the morning before they soften). Continue south on the PCT to the Trail 96 junction (~6,400 ft) and descend Trail 96 the way you came - back through Snowgrass Flat, across the Snowgrass Creek ford, past the spring/water source, and down through forest to the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead. No ropes, anchors, or rappel gear are needed for this route under normal summer conditions; a rope and basic glacier/snow travel gear are only warranted for early-season attempts with significant snow cover on the PCT traverse or summit scramble.
hazards: Loose rock and talus on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk to climbers below
Persistent snowfield on the PCT just below the summit that lingers into July and is a well-documented trouble spot for PCT thru-hikers; can be firm and icy in early morning
High wind and lightning exposure on the open crest, especially with July-August afternoon thunderstorms
Route-finding difficulty in poor visibility once you leave the PCT for the unmaintained summit spur/scree
Unreliable cell coverage throughout the Goat Rocks Wilderness

waysIn.name: Snowgrass Flat, the PCT north, and the unmarked climbers' path to the northwest ridge
waysIn.season: Roughly mid-Jul through Sep, most reliable in August
waysIn.notes:
From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead at about 4,600 ft at the end of the forest road, start on Trail 96. It climbs gently through forest, crossing Goat Creek on a footbridge at about 1.9 miles. When the Snowgrass Flats lot is full, park at Berry Patch Trailhead, about half a mile west along FR 2150 near Chambers Lake, where Trail 96 begins; it joins this route about 0.6 mile in, at the junction where the short hikers' path from the Snowgrass Flats lot comes in.

Around 2.4 to 2.6 miles you reach the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right, the last easy water before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek; there is no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except in heavy snowmelt.

Just beyond the ford at about 3.9-4 miles and 5,800 ft the trail breaks into the open heather meadows of Snowgrass Flat. Camping is prohibited within the flat itself under wilderness regulations; parties camp at designated sites above or below it.

Stay left where the bypass trail forks right at about 3.9 miles, continue straight past the Goat Lake trail junction at about 4.7 miles, and reach the PCT at about 5.4 miles and 6,400 ft; turn left, north. Follow the PCT about 1.8 miles across rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill on Old Snowy's west flank.

Round trip is roughly 15.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain, typically 8.5 to 9.5 hours car to car. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm before driving.
hazards: An unmarked, easily missed turn off the PCT — the route's one real navigation problem
A persistent snowfield on the PCT traverse below the summit, firm and icy in early morning
Loose rock and talus on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk to climbers below
High wind and lightning exposure on an open crest, with common afternoon thunderstorms
Route-finding difficulty in poor visibility once off the PCT
Unreliable cell coverage throughout the wilderness

name: Summit Block — North Face Direct Finish (variation)
approach: From the Hoh Rain Forest trailhead, follow the Hoh River Trail east through old-growth rainforest along the Hoh River. Established camps/toilets appear at roughly 5-Mile Island, the Olympus Guard Station (~9 mi, near the High Hoh Bridge), Lewis Meadow (~11 mi, 1,000 ft — the usual overnight on a 2-day approach, gravel bars/bear wire/privy), and Elk Lake (~15.5 mi) before the trail climbs steeply through forest to Glacier Meadows (17.3–17.4 mi, ~4,300 ft, community bear-wire, standard high camp). Watch for a washed-out, ladder-assisted cliffside stretch around mile 16 (rungs have been reported missing/broken in recent seasons), fallen-log stream crossings, and early-season steep snow on the lower trail calling for an axe; travel above Elk Lake carries avalanche exposure outside summer. Water is frequent the whole way. From Glacier Meadows a way-path climbs ~0.8 mi to the crest of the Blue Glacier's lateral moraine, then follows the moraine ~0.2 mi (steep, loose — some parties fix a short line) before dropping onto the ice; rope up here, crevasse-rescue kit mandatory. Cross the flat lower glacier and climb moderate snow, threading rock islands right of the main icefall before swinging back left below the massif, to Snow Dome (~6,600–6,800 ft), a common high camp ~1,000 ft below the summit. From Snow Dome most parties take the Crystal Pass line: up to and across Crystal Pass, then traverse just south of (below) Five Fingers Ridge, over a false summit, to the base of the true (West) summit block at ~7,900 ft on its northeast side, beneath the ~80 ft summit tower. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is usually snow-bridged through midsummer but can open late season; the steepest snow (~40–45°) has a clean runout in normal conditions, and a developing moat at the rock's base in warm/late-season conditions can force a committing step onto the rock.
descent: The North Face Direct Finish climbs straight up the ~80 ft north face on generally solid rock (5.4, one pitch) rather than the standard east-face ramp system — enough parties end up on this exact line that a semi-permanent rap anchor has built up at the top: a boulder/horn rigged with slings, a rap ring, and a quick link (inspect and back up any fixed tat, it is not agency-maintained). The rappel is roughly 80 to 100 ft from the summit down to the snow at the block's base — which a 60 m rope doubled (30 m/strand) reaches with room to spare. Bring a full 60 m rope, or plan to link two 30 m ropes, or use the lower intermediate station some parties have rigged to split it into two shorter rappels if carrying a shorter (30–40 m) rope. This single double-rope rappel lands you back on the snow essentially at the base of this finish. From there, reverse Crystal Pass, Snow Dome, the Blue Glacier and lateral moraine, and the Hoh River Trail back to the trailhead, typically with another night at Lewis Meadow or Elk Lake.
hazards: The North Face is steeper and more exposed than other summit block variations; early or late season may feature ice, making this variation significantly more dangerous

waysIn.name: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome to the base of the summit block
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Aug; early or late season this face can carry ice, which changes it from a 5.4 pitch into something else
waysIn.notes: Identical to the standard approach for every route on this peak: Hoh River Trail from the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center about 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at roughly 4,300 ft, the moraine way path and the drop onto the Blue Glacier, roped glacier travel across the flat lower ice and up through the rock islands right of the icefall to Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft, then Crystal Pass, the traverse below Five Fingers Ridge, the false summit, and the sharp saddle beneath the true summit pyramid. The only thing this route changes is what you do once you are standing at the foot of the tower.
hazards: Fixed tat at the top of the pitch is old and unmaintained — inspect and back it up
The face is steeper and more exposed than either other summit-block finish, and holds ice early and late in the season
The descent rappel is roughly 80-100 ft, which late in the season can take nearly all of a 60 m rope doubled
Everything on the approach: Blue Glacier crevasses, the Crystal Pass crevasse, moraine rockfall, whiteout on Snow Dome

name: Open Book
approach: Identical trailhead-to-basin approach as the Classic Route and The Roof: from the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, hike the maintained Snow Lake Trail ~1 mile (about 350 ft of up-and-down) to Snow Lake, the last water source. Continue past the lake on the fading tread over a wooded rise, then pick a line up and right into the talus/dirt gully on the peak's NW side; a climbers' path reappears on a heather bench near the gully's top and leads into the basin beneath the summit block. Ascend moraine along the edge of the small basin snowfield to the saddle (Unicorn Col) just west/southwest of the summit, then follow the use trail traversing below the cliffs on the south side of the peak to the base of the summit horn. The Open Book line starts at two wide, left-leaning cracks about 50 ft right of the Classic Route on the same south face, so from the base of the horn move climber's-right before starting the technical climbing; it's regarded as the easiest of the summit-block lines (Easy 5th class / 5.0), a step down from the Classic Route (5.4-5.6) and The Roof (5.6). Total approach is roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft gain, mostly on climbers' path and talus once past Snow Lake.
descent: From the top of the Open Book, either downclimb the same easy corner (viable given the route's easier grade, but still exposed near the top) or rappel using the same anchor system as the other summit-block routes: a large rock horn on the south side of the summit block, roughly 40-50 ft above the notch/base. Avoid the old dead tree/snag — it's reported as no longer trustworthy. A 30m rope is commonly reported as sufficient for the single-rope rappel, but multiple parties have found 30m to be marginal or just short depending on which of the two rappel lines off the horn you use (one reaches the south notch, the other drops toward the basin/glacier side), so a 40m rope removes any doubt. After reaching the ground, reverse the approach across the scree traverse, down through the basin and gully, past Snow Lake, and out the Snow Lake Trail.
hazards: Wide-crack climbing that feels awkward and poorly protected without large cams.
Loose rock is reported in the gully and chimney terrain around the summit tower.
Loose talus and scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out, usually by mid-to-late July.
Exposed step near the top of the summit horn with real air below on the block's east side.

waysIn.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the rightmost line on the summit horn
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Identical approach to the peak's other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, the maintained trail about a mile and roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake, the last water. Past the lake the tread fades over a wooded rise; work up and right into the talus and dirt gully on the northwest side, where a climbers' path reappears on a heather bench near the top and leads into the basin beneath the summit block. Ascend moraine along the edge of the small basin snowfield to Unicorn Col, then follow the traversing use trail below the cliffs on the south side to the base of the horn.

This route takes the right-hand end of the south face rather than the face direct, and it is the easiest of the three summit-block lines — a step down from the Classic Route and well below The Roof.

Roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft of gain, mostly on climbers' path and talus once past Snow Lake.
hazards: Wide-crack climbing that is awkward and poorly protected without large cams
Loose rock in the gully and chimney terrain around the summit tower
Loose talus and scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out
An exposed step near the top of the horn with real air below on the east side
A 30 m rope that may not reach on one of the two rappel lines

name: Southwest Slopes Scramble
approach: Trailhead: Slate Pass (~6,900 ft), the end of the Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) just below Slate Peak lookout — this is a full backpack approach, not a day hike (~13 miles/1,400+ ft one-way to base camp, within the ~28-mile round trip). From Slate Pass, drop off the pass on the old trail/way-trail toward the Whistler Cutoff Trail; this initial descent can hold snow well into summer (some parties carry an ice axe for it). The Whistler Cutoff Trail is an easy, well-graded downhill cruise to the Middle Fork Pasayten River, which is crossed unbridged — typically only ankle-to-shin deep in normal summer flow, but ford with care during early-season snowmelt or after rain. From the ford, join the Robinson Creek / Eureka Creek Trail system and follow it roughly to the Fred's Lake cutoff around the 9-10 mile mark; trail tread is in generally good, brush-free condition to this point. At the Shellrock Trail junction the maintained tread ends — travel beyond here is on a rougher, sometimes brushy path with blowdown. Climb past Fred's Lake to 7,100-ft Rolo (Fred's) Pass, then descend/contour a short, sometimes cliff-banded slope (route-find carefully here) into the Lake Doris basin (6,975 ft), a good camp with reliable water and the standard base camp for Osceola. From camp, leave the trail and go cross-country roughly 0.6 mile northeast through open forest, then talus, gaining about 1,400 ft up Osceola's long southwest-facing scree/talus slope to either the southwest ridge or south face. The south face is a slow, tedious boulder/talus slog; a faint but real climbers' trail on the southwest ridge (roughly 48.828, -120.583) offers noticeably better footing and is preferred by parties who've found it. Final scrambling to the 8,584 ft summit is Class 2-3. Watch for wet, lichen-covered rock on the upper slope, which gets slick fast in any moisture. In mid-July the trail to Lake Doris is in good shape, with a ford of the Middle Fork Pasayten and some blowdowns on the Eureka Creek trail.
descent: Walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling on this route (rappels: 0). Descend the same southwest-ridge climbers' trail or south-face talus/scree line used on the ascent back down to Lake Doris camp (about 1,400 ft of descent, roughly an hour); the ridge line is preferred over the direct south-face boulder field for better footing, especially on wet rock. From Lake Doris, reverse the full approach: climb back over 7,100-ft Rolo/Fred's Pass (mind the cliff-banded section just above the lake), pass Fred's Lake, pick up the Eureka/Robinson Creek Trail and Whistler Cutoff Trail, re-ford the Middle Fork Pasayten River, and climb back up to Slate Pass — roughly 13 miles and a full day's hiking each way, so most parties treat this as a 2-3 day backpack rather than a car-to-car push. No technical gear is needed for the descent beyond normal scrambling caution on loose scree and any lingering snow near Slate Pass. Descend the southwest ridge to the saddle, then drop scree back to your packs; this is easier than reversing the boulder field.
hazards: Loose, unstable talus and scree on the standard SW-slope route
Cliff bands wrap the north, east, and most other aspects of the peak — off-route terrain can cliff out
Early-season snowfields on the approach and lower peak (ice axe useful into early July)
Long, remote approach (10-13+ miles one-way) with no cell coverage — self-rescue is the default
Afternoon thunderstorms typical of the North Cascades east-slope summer climate
Black bear country — secure food storage required

waysIn.name: Slate Pass, the Middle Fork Pasayten, and Fred's Lake to Lake Doris
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the pass above Fred's Lake holds snow on its north side and softens through the day
waysIn.notes: Drive FR 5400 from Mazama to Harts Pass, at roughly 6,181 to 6,204 ft. Trailers are prohibited past the 5400000/5400060 junction because the road is narrow and steep with few turnouts, and whether an ordinary car should attempt it is genuinely disputed, so judge it on the day. From Harts Pass turn right at the guard station onto FR 5400-600. The Pacific Crest Trail trailhead is at the first switchback and Slate Pass at the second, at about 6,900 ft. Early in the season you walk the last half mile or so. From Slate Pass take the Buckskin Ridge trail #498, and at about half a mile a cut-off drops to the Robinson Creek / Middle Fork trail #478. Follow the Middle Fork of the Pasayten — an unbridged crossing, reported anywhere from ankle deep to needing boots and trousers off — for roughly nine miles to the Fred's Lake turn-off. The tread through here is in good condition with essentially no brush. Then over the pass to Lake Doris at about 6,975 ft, reported at just under six hours from the car. A naming caution before you cross-reference maps: this water is usually called Lake Doris and sometimes Lake Dorothy. Do not assume they are separate. Despite the route name, the ordinary way up this peak works the south or south-west slope, not a west one.
hazards: Unbridged Middle Fork Pasayten crossing of very variable depth
Blowdown that worsens beyond Fred's Lake, in places hundreds of logs through burn zones
Lingering snow on the north side of the pass above Fred's Lake, soft late in the day
Wet lichen making the talus slippery
Fourteen hundred feet of loose scree with no shelter

name: Southeast Route
approach: From the Goodell Creek trailhead (~600 ft, reached via the gravel road that forks off Hwy 20 across from Newhalem and dead-ends at a gravel pit — there's parking but no trailhead sign), follow the old abandoned logging roadbed paralleling the true-left/east bank of Goodell Creek. The first ~1.5 miles thread through dozens of downed trees and washouts on the roadbed before a real, if faint, trail emerges in the timber above; tread then levels out around 1,100 ft for roughly a mile. Around mile 3.5 (~1,700 ft) the trail crosses a stream — the last easy, reliable water for a long stretch — near a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path up 'The Barrier,' the forested spur ridge that separates the Goodell/Terror Creek drainage from Crescent Creek Basin; fill bottles here. From the cairn the path steepens hard: a traverse around 3,200 ft, a talus field near 4,000 ft, a rock band around 4,800 ft, then a steep, brush-choked gully (early-season snow/ice up to ~35°) to a rocky streambed near 5,200 ft. Above that, heather benches and slabs lead to the crest of The Barrier, a ~6,200 ft notch that is the high point of the approach and the site of a common bivy. From the notch, descend ~250 ft into 'Stump Hollow,' the gentle basin between The Barrier and the Chopping Block, then contour on a long, rising traverse across the snow, slabs, and talus of Crescent Creek Basin — holding roughly the 5,800 ft level — to a camp near Mount Terror/Himmelhorn (around 7-9 miles and 6,000-6,500 ft of gain from the trailhead, consistent with this route's ~28 km round-trip distance). From camp, continue the rising traverse of Crescent Creek Basin toward the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col; crampon up the final snow/scree pitch to the col itself, which turns to loose, chossy class 3-4 scrambling once melted out late-season, with an overhanging boulder near the top sometimes forcing a chossy class 3/4 bypass on the left. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required. Both The Barrier crossing and the basin traverse involve real route-finding on an unsigned, easily-lost climbers' path through heather and talus, and creek crossings near the trailhead can run high and fast on hot, high-snowmelt afternoons.
descent: Descend the Southeast Route by reversing the east ridge back down to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col — a few pitches of low-5th-class downclimbing/scrambling to the notch. From the col, the standard return for this route is down the south side, back into Crescent Creek Basin: this is the easier, non-technical line (snow early season, loose class 3-4 talus/scree scrambling once late-season melt strips the snow) and does not require rappelling under normal conditions. If coverage is thin and a section of the loose downclimb feels too exposed, some parties back it off with a single short rappel off a sling on a natural anchor (block/horn) rather than downclimb it, but this is not the norm. Note that the north side of the col is a different, and harder, proposition and is not part of this route's own descent — parties continuing a traverse toward Himmelhorn/Mustard Glacier descend that side via one single-rope rappel from an established rap station about 150 ft below the col onto the Mustard Glacier (or, when well filled-in, a steep snow couloir); don't confuse that crossing with the Southeast Route's own walk-off. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: traverse back to the base of The Barrier, regain the ~250 ft to the 6,200 ft notch, then descend the steep gully/talus/heather line back down to the Goodell Creek trail and out to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully below the Barrier notch and for creek crossings running high on hot afternoons. To continue on to Frenzel Spitz, descend roughly 500 ft from Ottohorn's north side, per the original 1961 first-ascent account.
hazards: loose rock
routefinding
remoteness
afternoon weather

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek, the Barrier notch and Stump Hollow, then the Crescent Creek Basin traverse to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the gravel road that forks off Hwy 20 across from Newhalem and dead-ends at a gravel pit with parking but no trailhead sign, follow the old logging roadbed along the east bank of Goodell Creek. The first 1.5 miles thread through dozens of downed trees and washouts before a faint trail emerges in the timber; the tread then levels around 1,100 ft for roughly a mile.

Around mile 3.5, at about 1,700 ft, the trail crosses a stream, the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, near a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path up the Barrier. Fill bottles there.

From the cairn the path steepens hard: a traverse around 3,200 ft, a talus field near 4,000 ft, a rock band around 4,800 ft, then a steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees, to a rocky streambed near 5,200 ft. Heather benches and slabs then lead to the crest of the Barrier, a roughly 6,200 ft notch that is the high point of the approach and a common bivy. From the notch, descend about 250 ft into Stump Hollow, then contour on a long rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin holding roughly the 5,800 ft level to a camp near Mount Terror and Himmelhorn.

A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required.
hazards: A steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees on the Barrier climb
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose exposed bypass
A moat at the col that can become an overhanging pit by August
A fresh rockfall scar reported about 30 ft below the summit ridge
The north side of the col takes multiple rappels off improvised anchors; do not descend it by mistake
Steep grassy ledges on the Barrier that are considerably worse downhill-facing and tired

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Park at the Eagle Creek/Oval trailhead (~3,000 ft) at the end of FR 4420-080, reached via Twisp River Road/FR 44 (~12.5 mi west of Twisp) and the West Buttermilk/FR 4420 spur. From the trailhead, follow Eagle Creek Trail #410 for about 1.9 miles up the Eagle Creek valley (trail parallels the creek, so water is available) to the signed junction with Oval Creek Trail #410A. Bear onto #410A and climb steadily through forest along Oval Creek for roughly 7.5 more miles, passing West Oval Lake before reaching Middle Oval Lake (~6,700-6,800 ft) — about 9.5 miles and ~4,400 ft of gain from the car; there is good established camping near the lake's outflow if splitting the trip over two days. From the outflow, leave the maintained tread and scramble cross-country up open talus/scree slopes to the north/northeast to gain the Sawtooth crest at a broad saddle roughly 1,200-1,500 ft above the lake, then follow the rocky crest generally north/northwest over blocky, sometimes loose talus to Oval Peak's summit block.
