Much of this basin burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire, so the lower trail is exposed, dry, and dusty in summer with sections of soft/fragile burned ground that can give way underfoot — carry all the water you'll need once you leave Middle Oval Lake, since there are no reliable sources higher up. The crest scramble is class 2 but has real route-finding and loose-rock exposure in poor visibility.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb/scramble back along the Sawtooth crest talus to the saddle above Middle Oval Lake, then drop the scramble slope back down to the lake's outflow and rejoin the maintained Oval Creek Trail #410A. Retrace the ~7.5 miles down through the Oval Lakes basin (past West Oval Lake) to the junction with Eagle Creek Trail #410, and follow that 1.9 miles back to the trailhead. This is a class 2 talus/scree walk-down with no technical rappelling required in either direction — the main descent hazards are loose blocky talus on the crest (twisted-ankle/rockfall terrain, especially with other parties below) and the fragile burned tread lower on the trail. rappels: 0.
hazards: Extensive loose talus and scree across the entire upper mountain
Rockfall from parties above or from loose rock underfoot
Route-finding difficulty among similar-looking gullies/ribs near the summit
High, cold creek crossings on Eagle/Oval Creek during early-season (June) snowmelt
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above treeline
No reliable water above the Oval Lakes

waysIn.name: Oval Creek trail to Middle Oval Lake
waysIn.season: July to early October; best Aug-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the Eagle Creek road end, about two miles of valley trail reaches the Oval Creek fork, and seven and a half more miles of steady forest and old burn lead past the lower lake to Middle Oval Lake at just under 7,000 ft. There is established camping at the outflow, and splitting the trip in two there is the usual plan. Much of the lower basin burned and the tread is dry, dusty and shadeless with sections of soft ground that give underfoot. Carry everything you will drink above the lake — there is nothing reliable higher. Early in the season the Eagle and Oval Creek crossings run high and cold. There is no single defined line up this peak so much as several interchangeable ridge and slope options that converge near the top, and parties commonly go up one and down another for better footing.
hazards: Loose talus and large slick boulders across the whole upper mountain — twisted-ankle terrain rather than technical
Rockfall from parties above and from blocks that shift underfoot
Several similar-looking gullies and ribs near the summit, hard to tell apart in cloud
High, cold creek crossings during early-season snowmelt
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above treeline
No reliable water above the lakes

name: East Face
approach: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead (end of FR 56, Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road), the fastest approach uses the gated continuation of the road as a mountain-bike/hike-in: roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed (NF-5620) to Hardscrabble Horse Camp near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead, saving significant time over walking it. From there, follow the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River / Dutch Miller Gap Trail (Trail 1030) east along the north bank of the river for several more miles — the tread here is in reasonable shape with minimal blowdown, passing dispersed camps and, in season, overgrown thimbleberry brush that obscures footing on the lower tread. Roughly 13-14 miles in from the trailhead (about a mile before the trail crosses toward Williams Lake/Dutch Miller Gap proper), leave the trail and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River — a real ford, potentially thigh-to-waist deep and cold with snowmelt, so time it for lower water and expect wet feet. On the far side, climb steep, brushy forest into the rocky defile some parties call the 'Valley of the Chiefs,' a roughly two-mile corridor that gains the bench below Overcoat Peak. Continuous snowfields typically begin around 4,600 ft; above about 6,600 ft the route alternates between rock and snow, with one sloping, exposed rock step that requires care to downclimb onto steep snow. A common camp is on rock slabs/benches around 6,600 ft directly overlooking the Overcoat Glacier, roughly 100 ft below the glacier's toe. Total trailhead-to-camp distance is on the order of 15-16 miles with 5,000+ ft of gain; this is a serious, mostly off-trail approach through wilderness terrain (Alpine Lakes Wilderness) with real route-finding, so a GPS track or careful map work for the Valley of the Chiefs and glacier-bench section is worthwhile. From camp, traverse west across the mellow lower-angle part of the Overcoat Glacier to reach the base of a snow finger on the peak's north/east side that leads to the summit rock.
descent: Reverse the ascent for most parties: from the summit, downclimb the Class 3-4 gully/ledge system on the peak's east side back toward the snow finger and glacier. Where the ledges pinch down at a dihedral feature (a damp, water-streaked corner reported by climbers), most parties do NOT free-downclimb the full corner — instead, build two rappels (roughly full 30m/60m-rope-length pitches) down the dihedral to regain the glacier below. Anchors are natural (slung horns, chockstones, or gear placements) rather than fixed bolts/chains — this is an alpine line with no fixed hardware, so carry a small rack and cordage for anchor-building and expect to leave gear (or plan to down-lead/simul on lower-angle sections to save equipment). A single 60m rope handles both rappels; parties without a 60m would need to break it into more, shorter rappels. Some parties instead find they can downclimb the full gully/ledge system without rappelling if conditions and confidence allow (reversing the ascent by downclimbing is the lower-commitment option), but the two-rappel dihedral descent is the more commonly reported method, especially when the rock is wet or holds are snow-covered. Below the glacier, retrace the approach: descend the Valley of the Chiefs (or, as at least one party has done, an alternate line down the main Overcoat drainage through open trees to avoid waterfall-forming cliffs lower down), re-ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and rejoin the Dutch Miller Gap Trail back to Hardscrabble Horse Camp and the bike/hike-out to Dingford Creek Trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully/dihedral and for the river ford being higher/colder in the afternoon on hot days from glacier/snowmelt runoff.
hazards: Crevasses on the Overcoat Glacier, especially as snow bridges thin later in summer
Steep moats where the glacier pulls away from the rock late in the season
Loose rock in the summit gully and on the ledges below it
Exposed class 4 (occasionally low 5th-class) climbing on the final summit block
Long, brushy approach with downed trees and rocks hidden under thimbleberry on the old Dutch Miller Gap trailbed
Heavy mosquitoes at valley camps (e.g., Bears Breast tarns) in early-mid summer

waysIn.name: Dingford Creek, bike the closed road, then ford the Middle Fork under the big cliff
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The river ford is the timing constraint — thigh deep in the morning has been recorded as waist deep on the same day by evening
waysIn.notes: From I-90 exit 34 go north, then right onto SE Middle Fork Road, FR 56, and follow it about twelve miles to the Taylor River junction. Bear right onto FR 5620 and continue to the Dingford Creek trailhead at roughly 1,500 ft. FR 56 is notorious for potholes and ruts and high clearance is genuinely useful; the stretch beyond the gate is reported to be in better shape than the public road. FR 5620 is decommissioned beyond Dingford Creek. The closed stretch to the old Dutch Miller Gap trailhead and Hardscrabble Horse Camp is given as seven, eight or ten miles, so do not plan on a precise number. A bike is universally recommended and cuts hours off both ends. Beyond the road, parties use three genuinely different lines, none of them confirmed by another, so read all three before choosing. The most specific of them fords the Middle Fork on a visual cue rather than a mileage: walk roughly four miles of trail until you can see the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the foot of Overcoat. Push through about ten minutes of alder, ford there, and you land on the talus field at the base of those cliffs. Further north-east the alder gets much thicker. A second line crosses about a mile before the Dutch Miller Gap trail proper and climbs steep forest to camp at Overcoat Lake. A third crosses the river on rocks, climbs steep brushy ground into a two-mile rocky corridor sometimes called the Valley of the Chiefs, meets continuous snow around 4,600 ft, and goes over a pass at about 6,140 ft. On the traverse toward camp, one party's correction: they climbed to the ridge and then realised the line stays lower, and had to drop back to find the sloping rock crux and downclimb to the snow. A durable warning about the road rather than the mountain: the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road has a long-standing reputation for unsavoury activity, including gunfire, and at least one regular visitor reports it on every trip.
hazards: A real ford of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, thigh to waist deep and colder in the afternoon than the morning
Dense slide alder on both banks, worse to the north-east of the standard crossing
Moats around the margin of the Overcoat Glacier
Crevasses part way up the snow finger
Poor protection and loose rock on the summit pyramid
A long decommissioned road walk or ride at both ends of the day

name: Painted Mountain Scramble
approach: Park at the Sloan Creek Campground / North Fork Sauk trailhead (2,100 ft) at the end of FR 49. The signed trail here is the North Fork Sauk Trail #649, but the Painted Mountain route splits off almost immediately: look for the signed 'Red Mountain Trail' (a.k.a. Painted Mountain Lookout Trail) branching left about 100 yards in from the trailhead. Follow this boot path steadily uphill through forest for about 1 mile, gaining roughly 1,000 ft to where the maintained tread ends around 3,100 ft — this is the last reliable, easy-to-follow section. From 3,100 ft the route turns into a genuine scramble: climb a short but steep ~70-foot band of rock ledges covered in dirt and moss (roughly Class 3, the crux of the lower route — treat it as insecure, especially if wet) to gain the southwest ridge. Above the ledges the path thins to an intermittent boot track marked intermittently with old pink flagging; stay on the crest/southwest side of the ridge through open, flower-strewn meadows. Around 5,800 ft the visible path effectively disappears at an overlook above Ruby Lake — this is the key route-finding checkpoint; from here the line continues up steepening terrain (~300 ft of gain) staying on the right (west) side of the ridge crest. At about 6,700 ft you squeeze through a last band of stunted trees (again flagged with pink ribbon); above this there is no more ground cover, and the final several hundred feet to the 6,975-ft summit is loose scree and blocky rock. There is no reliable water past the trailhead/lower creek crossings, so carry what you need from the car; this is dry, south-facing, sun-exposed terrain in the upper half. Loose rock and scree-on-slab underfoot are the main hazards throughout the upper ridge, along with route-finding in fog since the flagging is sparse and the path is not maintained.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling on the standard route and no fixed anchors are known to exist on the peak. Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: pick your way back down the loose scree and blocky rock below 6,700 ft, drop back through the flagged tree band, then follow the intermittent, pink-ribbon-marked boot path back down the southwest ridge past the Ruby Lake overlook (~5,800 ft) to the top of the Class 3 ledge band around 3,100 ft. Downclimb the ~70-foot dirt-and-moss ledge section facing in where it feels exposed (this is the spot most parties find harder in descent than ascent, and where loose rock underfoot is most consequential), then rejoin the maintained tread of the Red Mountain/Painted Mountain Lookout Trail for the easy 1-mile walk back to the North Fork Sauk trailhead. Total round trip is about 8 miles with roughly 4,875 ft of gain/loss, so budget a full day; the biggest descent hazards are loose talus/scree on the upper ridge and losing the faint path in poor visibility, not technical rope work.
hazards: Exposed Class 2-3 ledge scramble (~70 vertical ft) just above the end of the maintained trail at 3,100 ft -- loose dirt-on-rock, slick when wet
Faint, unmaintained boot path above the ledges marked only by intermittent pink flagging -- easy to lose in fog or low visibility
Loose scree/talus on the upper southwest ridge and summit slopes
Lingering snow on the ledges and ridge into July in heavy-snow years, which can hide the flagged path and make the ledges icy
Open, exposed ridge with no shelter from summer afternoon thunderstorms
No reliable water beyond Ruby Lake basin/creek crossings

waysIn.name: Sloan Creek Road, the lookout trail, and the southwest ridge
waysIn.season: Late July through September is the reliable window. Snow can linger on the ledges and the ridge boot path into July in heavy-snow years, hiding the flagging and icing the ledges. The scramble is far safer and easier to navigate dry.
waysIn.notes: Park at the campground and trailhead at the end of the road up the North Fork Sauk. The signed trail there is the valley trail, but this route splits off almost immediately: look for the signed lookout trail branching left about a hundred yards in. It is low-key enough to walk straight past — if you have been on the main trail more than a couple of minutes you have missed it. The lookout trail switchbacks steadily through old growth for about a mile, gaining roughly seven hundred to a thousand feet, and ends on a flat bench where the fire lookout once stood, with views into the basin below. That is the last easy-to-follow section of the day and where most hikers turn around. Above it the path keeps climbing steeply and a cliff band appears within a few hundred vertical feet. Beyond the cliff band, an intermittent boot track marked with old pink flagging follows the crest and southwest side of the ridge through open meadows. There is no reliable water past the lower creek crossings, and the upper half is dry, south-facing and sun-exposed, so carry what you need from the car.
hazards: an exposed ledge scramble of about seventy vertical feet just above the end of the maintained trail — loose dirt on rock, slick when wet, and harder facing outward on descent
a faint, unmaintained boot path above the ledges marked only by intermittent pink flagging, easy to lose in fog
loose scree and talus on the upper southwest ridge and summit slopes
lingering snow that can hide the flagged path into July
an open, exposed ridge with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
no reliable water above the lower creek crossings

name: Standard Rock Route
approach: From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff (directly across the highway from the Wine Spires), a boot/climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop (can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt), and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The trail gains steeply and steadily — on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles — to a broad, flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps; this bench is the last reliable water (small tarns/creek trickle, can run dry by late summer — treat before drinking). From the bench, continue up the main climbers' trail over steep talus and scree to Burgundy Col, which holds three or four bivy sites with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties. From the col, cross to the east side and traverse south over snow and talus at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin, below the east walls of Chianti and Pernod. From below the east walls, climb obliquely up and around to the notch between Chianti and Pernod; this section runs to roughly three pitches of mostly 4th and 5th class. Lingering snow on the east side into early July may call for an axe and light traction.
descent: This is a rappel descent, not a walk-off. Rappel from the summit block back to the notch between Pernod and Chianti, then make long rappels down the east side to the snow and névé at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin. No rappel count is published for this line; carry double ropes, and cord to back up or replace old slings and bolts. From the glacier edge, traverse back north below Chianti and climb a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' trail (scree, the bench, then the timbered rib) to the SR-20 pullout. Watch for moats along the rock late in the season, and budget real time for the loose scree below the col.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall potential in the approach gullies, at the col, and around the summit notch
Lingering snow and glacier-fringe travel crossing toward the Silver Star Glacier into July
Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer
Aging FA-era fixed pitons/bolts on route — inspect and back up rather than trust blindly

waysIn.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then across the east side to the Pernod–Chianti notch
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes: From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, directly across the highway from the Wine Spires, a boot and climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop, and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The creek can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt. The trail gains steeply and steadily, on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles, to a broad flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps. This bench is the last reliable water: small tarns and a creek trickle that can run dry by late summer. Above it the trail climbs steep talus and scree to Burgundy Col, the usual camp for this climb. From the col the route crosses to the east side of the spires and traverses south below their east walls to reach the notch between Chianti and Pernod.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the climb to Burgundy Col
Snow and névé at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin on the east side, with moats along the rock late in the season
Roughly three pitches of mostly 4th and 5th class to reach the notch
A rappel descent back down the east side, followed by a re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Old first-ascent bolts on the summit block; carry cord to back up or replace old slings
The bench is the last reliable water and can run dry by late summer

name: South Route
approach: There are two real approach options for the South (Southwest) Route on Phantom Peak, and both are serious multi-day North Cascades bushwhacks — this is not a trail hike. Option one, the Luna Creek approach: from Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake (roughly $35, saves about 6 miles of paddling/road-walking) to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it's about 9-10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage (through old-growth cedar groves and past beaver ponds/marshy sections) to Luna Camp, an established backcountry campsite where a NOCA wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends; climbers leave the maintained tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom Peak's south side, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Fred Beckey, on the first traverse through here in 1940, found it a brutal fight through flies, devil's club, willows, and alder — modern parties confirm little has changed, reporting huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder so dense that 0.5 mph is a good pace, plus heavy mosquito/fly pressure in summer. The creek itself must be forded in places; fords get harder (deeper, faster) the lower/farther downstream you are, so it's best to gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as possible rather than fighting the brush along the creek itself. Water is abundant throughout (the creek and countless side-seeps), but hazard is really the terrain: no trail, no cairns, high fall-into-a-hole-in-the-brush risk, and real potential to get separated from a partner in the thick stuff (this has happened to real parties here). Above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. Option two, favored by several recent parties, comes from the north via Whatcom Pass: Hannegan Trailhead (3,100 ft) → Hannegan Pass Trail → Chilliwack River Trail (includes a cable-car creek crossing) → Brush Creek Trail up to Whatcom Pass, then off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From that camp, the route to Phantom itself is a roughly 1,000-ft descending traverse east across snow/talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress — this saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing. Whichever approach is used, expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
descent: Standard practice is to reverse the ascent line rather than walk off a different way — there is no easy alternate descent gully on this peak. From the true summit, downclimb back across the false-summit ridge crest (using a hand line on the short, exposed step above the false summit if the party fixed one on the way up), then down the broken Class 2-3 rock slope to the top of the snow finger. This is also where you'll retrieve any snow flukes or pickets placed as running protection on the ascent — plan on down-climbing/down-tooling the snow finger and re-crossing the bergschrund via the same slabby rock step used going up. Below the bergschrund, descend the pocket glacier and snowfield back to the ~6,100-ft saddle in the southwest buttress, then reverse the ~1,000-ft traverse back to camp (Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine, if approached from Whatcom Pass) or continue down into the Luna Creek drainage to regain the brush and, eventually, the Big Beaver Trail. The one place real rappelling is recorded on this route is the short, steep summit tower/rock step just below the true summit: the 1959 second-ascent party (Josendal, Sharpe, Spickard) found downclimbing was not comfortable there and made two rappels down a roughly 150-ft cliff band on the east side of the summit ridge to get past it. Given the remote, rarely-visited, and reportedly 'somewhat rotten' rock in this gully/tower section, expect natural anchors only — slung horns or rock threads, not bolts — so carry a small rack of slings/cord for building anchors. A single 60m rope handles the two ~75-ft rappels comfortably (or two 30m/60m ropes if the party prefers not to pull and re-rig). Total descent time from summit back to a southwest-buttress base camp has been reported at around 5-6 hours by a party climbing this line. Overall hazard on descent is exposure and loose rock on the tower/gully sections, plus the same bergschrund and snow-finger objective hazards (crevasse fall, rockfall off the buttress walls) encountered on the way up, and — once back down in the trees — the same brutal, disorienting Luna Creek brush that makes the whole approach infamous.
hazards: Bergschrund crossing on the pocket glacier below the SW buttress
Loose, broken Class 2-3 rock above the schrund
False summit adds real route-finding risk in fog/whiteout
Fast-moving fog and generally fickle North Cascades weather
Extremely brutal, insect-plagued bushwhack if approaching via Luna Creek

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
waysIn.season: Late Jun-Aug
waysIn.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
hazards: Chilliwack cable-car crossing and Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
About 1,000 ft descending traverse across snow and talus to the buttress, to be regained on the return
Bergschrund on the pocket glacier, crossed via a slabby rock step; crevasse fall risk
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully; natural anchors only
False summit and exposed ridge crest: route-finding risk in fog or whiteout
Fast-moving fog and fickle weather; 2-3 days of travel each way

waysIn.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side
waysIn.season: Late Jun-Aug
waysIn.notes: From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 9 to 10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, about half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder lower down and farther downstream
Risk of falling into holes hidden in the brush and of separating from a partner
No trail and no cairns; disorienting on the way back down
Bergschrund on the pocket glacier, crossed via a slabby rock step; rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower; false summit and exposed ridge crest in fog
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
waysIn.whyThisWay: When starting from SR-20 and wanting the shortest, flattest way into the Pickets; the water taxi and Big Beaver trail are easy, but the last stretch up Luna Creek is a pathless bushwhack.

name: West Ridge
approach: An involved two-day approach: ~10 miles on trail up and over Hannegan Pass, wading the Chilliwack River, traversing the scenic 5-mile Easy Ridge, soloing exposed 4th-class terrain across the 'Imperfect Impasse,' climbing through Perfect Pass and over the Challenger Glacier, then descending and traversing steep snow, talus, and more glacier to a bivy site under Ghost Peak (Phantom Peak's neighbor immediately to the north), from which the full west ridge comes into view.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the southeast face, including a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall (the FA party noted this crossing would be more straightforward earlier in the season, with more snow cover), circling back to the bivy camp under Ghost Peak.
hazards: Wildfire smoke has affected the approach corridor and return route in past seasons
Rockfall on the descent snowfield
Towers along the ridge require route-finding to bypass or climb directly

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier to a bivy under Ghost Peak
waysIn.season: Jul-Aug
waysIn.notes:
An involved two-day approach. Roughly 10 miles on trail up and over Hannegan Pass, wading the Chilliwack River, then the scenic 5-mile traverse of Easy Ridge, soloing exposed 4th-class terrain across the Imperfect Impasse, climbing through Perfect Pass and over the Challenger Glacier, then descending and traversing steep snow, talus and more glacier to a bivy site.

The route was first climbed in July 2021 and is documented in a single first-ascent account, so treat everything about it as sparsely reported.
hazards: The Imperfect Impasse, soloed as exposed 4th class on the way in
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier
A rockfall-exposed snowfield crossing on the descent, worse later in the season
A single published ascent, so no accumulated route-finding knowledge to fall back on
Wading the Chilliwack River

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Park at the Lake Serene Trailhead (from Hwy 2 ~21 mi east of Monroe, turn onto FR 6020, then FR 6020-109; Northwest Forest Pass required, two outhouses at the lot) and start up Lake Serene Trail #1068, a well-graded, heavily-used maintained trail through second-growth forest. At roughly 1.6 miles a signed junction splits off a short spur to Bridal Veil Falls — stay right/uphill for Lake Serene. Shortly after, the trail crosses Bridal Veil Creek on a long footbridge (last easy, reliable water before the lake) and begins a sustained set of switchbacks, gaining about 1,900 ft over the next two miles. Around 3.5 miles and ~1,920 ft of gain (roughly 2-2.5 hrs at a moderate pace) the trail levels out at Lake Serene's outlet, marked by a toilet/outhouse sign — this is where the maintained tread ends and the scramble begins. There is no established bootpath up Philadelphia: most parties backtrack a couple hundred feet down the trail, then cut uphill into a brushy boulder field on the south side of the lake (the first ~50 ft is the worst of it) to gain the ridge above the lake's south shore. Follow that ridge crest southeast, trending close to the cliff edge above the lake (exposed, view-heavy but with real fall potential) before the angle eases through forest thick with slide alder, blowdown, and moss-slick rock. At about 3,200 ft the ridge bends east and merges into the broader west ridge of Philadelphia Mountain — a mostly timbered, Class 2 walk with a few small meadow openings — which climbs the final ~1,000 ft over roughly a mile of undulating, multi-false-summit terrain to the flat, viewless top (4,258 ft). Hazards: no path or cairns to follow (route-finding is entirely on the party), dense brush and downed timber low on the ridge, mossy rock that's slick when wet, and lingering snow into late spring — many parties intentionally time this climb for a continuous snowpack specifically to bury the brush, which trades bushwhacking for steeper, more exposed snow travel above the lake and minor avalanche/cornice considerations on that slope. Partway up the west ridge, work around a cliff band by trending left (north) rather than pushing straight through it — the cliffs are on the south side of this upper ridge, and this is the spot parties most often get stuck. Note that the handedness flips at the bend: lower down, the drop is on the north, into the lake. In April the bootpath leaves the main trail just before the outhouse at the lake outlet and is easy to miss; without it the brush on the slope above is thick with devils club.
descent: This is a walk-off with no rappelling — Class 2 terrain the entire way, reversing the ascent line. From the summit, retrace the undulating west ridge back down to about 3,200 ft, then drop off the ridge into the brushy boulder field above Lake Serene's south shore, working carefully back down to the lake outlet where the maintained Lake Serene Trail resumes at the toilet sign. From there it's a straightforward, well-graded trail descent (about 2-2.5 hrs) back down the switchbacks, across the Bridal Veil Creek footbridge, past the falls spur junction, and out to the trailhead. The trickiest part of the descent is actually the off-trail section: losing the correct line off the ridge into the boulder field is the most common way parties end up cliffed out above the lake or pushed into thicker brush than necessary, so retracing the ascent track (visually or via GPS breadcrumbs) is the standard mitigation, and the mossy rock and brush that were merely awkward on the way up become more hazardous descending wet or loaded with a pack. In early-season snow, short glissades on the upper ridge are common but should be done well back from the exposed drop toward the lake.
hazards: Slide-alder brush and downed timber on the off-trail west ridge
Moss-covered boulders that are slick even when dry, worse when wet
Loss of route in fog/low cloud since there is no trail or cairned line above Lake Serene
Winter/spring snow that can hide holes in the boulder field and load the steeper sections near the cliff band

waysIn.name: Lake Serene outlet to the west ridge
waysIn.season: June to October, or under snow
waysIn.notes: Shares the busiest day-hike in the valley for its first three and a half miles: gently graded tread to the Bridal Veil Falls spur junction, then the long footbridge over Bridal Veil Creek — the last easy water — and a sustained set of switchbacks gaining most of the day's trail elevation over the next two miles. The maintained tread ends abruptly at the lake outlet by the toilet sign, and there is no established boot path onto the peak beyond it. Under continuous snowpack the whole line is markedly easier, which is why many parties save it for winter.
hazards: Slide alder and heavy blowdown on the off-trail ridge
Moss-covered boulders that are slick even when dry
A cliff band on the upper west ridge, turned on the north (left) side — the cliffs are south here
Real fall potential where the crest runs along the drop above the lake
No cairned line to follow in fog, and several convincing false tops

name: Pinnacle Saddle / South Gully
approach: From the Pinnacle Peak Trailhead — a signed, unnumbered NPS trail directly across Stevens Canyon Road from the Reflection Lakes parking pullouts (trailhead elevation ~4,860 ft) — the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail climbs at a steady, fairly steep grade through sparse subalpine forest. Around 0.5 mile you get the first partial view of Rainier through the trees; the trail then switchbacks up through subalpine meadow terrain. At about 1.25–1.3 miles and roughly 1,000–1,050 ft of gain you top out at Pinnacle Saddle (~5,900–5,920 ft), the notch between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak, where the maintained trail ends and the view opens south to Mount Adams, St. Helens, and Hood. Carry water from the car — there's no reliable source on the trail or in the gully above except lingering snowmelt early in the season. Past the saddle you leave the maintained tread and the route becomes an unmaintained climbers'/boot path: contour or scramble east into the gully system on the peak's south/southeast face. The rock is old, variable-quality lava flow — solid in spots, rotten in others — so test holds and watch for loose blocks, especially with parties above or below. The gully starts as Class 2 scree and blocky steps, steepening into sustained Class 3 scrambling with real exposure over its upper third, working through a band of trees before a final short scramble to the summit block at 6,562 ft. Snow or verglas can linger in the gully into July on colder years, which turns easy scrambling into a genuine hazard — an ice axe (and willingness to turn around) is worth carrying in early season. Afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the Tatoosh in summer and this route is fully exposed on an open ridge, so plan to be off the summit by early afternoon.
descent: For the standard Class 2–3 scramble, the descent is the same gully used on ascent, back down to Pinnacle Saddle and out the maintained trail to Reflection Lakes — most parties downclimb the whole thing rather than rope up, and this is a walk-off/downclimb route, not a rappel route, in normal summer conditions. That said, the upper gully has a short, sustained Class 3 step with enough exposure that some parties choose to protect or rappel it rather than downclimb, particularly when the rock is wet or in early-season snow: a single ~40 ft rappel off a sling/natural anchor (block, horn, or small cam placement — there is no fixed/bolted anchor) gets you past the crux, after which the remaining scree gully back to the saddle is a straightforward downclimb. Carry a 30m or half a 60m rope and a few slings/small cams if you want this option in your back pocket rather than commit to a sketchy downclimb. Note this is distinct from the separate steeper winter/snow line up the same gully system (climbed with pickets, sometimes 1–2 short roped pitches near the top), which is descended by rappelling the gully on natural gear anchors — that is a different, more technical undertaking than the summer scramble covered here.
hazards: Loose, unstable rock in the south-facing summit gully — NPS itself calls the scramble above the saddle 'a precipitous scramble on loose, unstable rock'
Steep dropoffs and exposure along sections of the maintained trail, not just on the scramble above the saddle
Snow can linger in the summit gully into early-to-mid summer even after the approach trail has melted out, requiring traction/an ice axe
Sudden afternoon thunderstorms are common on this exposed south Cascades ridge in summer
Rockfall risk onto parties below on the gully given how heavily traveled the route is
No water sources anywhere along the trail or scramble
Habituated mountain goats frequent the saddle and surrounding ridges seeking salt from sweat and urine

waysIn.name: Pinnacle Saddle and the south gully

Carry water from the car; there is no reliable source on the trail or in the gully except lingering snowmelt early in the season. Past the saddle the route becomes an unmaintained climbers' path. The rock is old, variable-quality lava flow — solid in places and rotten in others — so test holds and watch for loose blocks with parties above or below. This is a fully exposed ridge with quick-building afternoon thunderstorms in summer; plan to be off the summit by early afternoon.
hazards: Loose, unstable rock through the south-facing summit gully
Steep dropoffs and exposure on sections of the maintained trail itself, not only above the saddle
Snow lingering in the summit gully into early or mid summer after the trail has melted out
Rockfall onto parties below on a heavily travelled line
Sudden afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed south Cascades ridge
No water anywhere on the trail or the scramble

name: Pinnacle Saddle / North Slopes
approach: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road (1.4 miles east of the Paradise-Longmire Road junction, roughly 1.9 miles from the Paradise turnoff). The signed Pinnacle Peak Trail (no official trail number; it's a Mount Rainier NP maintained trail) leaves from the south side of the road, directly across from the largest of the Reflection Lakes (approx. 46.7683, -121.7314). The trail climbs moderately through mountain hemlock and Alaska yellow cedar forest for the first half-mile; around 0.5 mi you get a first partial view of Rainier through the trees, and at about 0.6 mi you cross a seasonal stream/cascading creek that is the only reliable water on the hike (dry by late summer in low-snow years). By 0.7 mi the trail breaks out of forest into open talus and heather slopes below the cliffs of Pinnacle Peak, and steepens noticeably from here — this is where lingering snow (well into July on the shaded, north-facing switchbacks) creates the trail's main hazard, since a slip on hard morning snow above the talus can slide a hiker into rock. Around 0.9-1.0 mi the trail passes beneath the impressive cliff bands on Pinnacle's north face, then switchbacks up a short, exposed final pitch (the trail's best viewpoint) to reach Pinnacle/Pinnacle Saddle (Pinnacle Gap) at about 1.25-1.3 mi and roughly 5,920-5,960 ft. This saddle is the trail's official end and the crux junction: unmaintained user paths fork east toward Pinnacle Peak/The Castle and west toward Plummer and Denman peaks. For Plummer Peak, continue a short distance past the saddle and look for a climbers' path branching right (west); it crosses a flat rocky shelf holding a seasonal tarn, where a fork continues straight toward Denman — instead bear left (south/uphill) onto the boot path that climbs the open, rocky north-facing slopes of Plummer Peak. This upper section is unmaintained, loose in spots, and route-finding is straightforward but the tread is thin; a short class 2-3 scramble (brief hands-on-rock moves, some loose blocks, mild exposure) gains the last few hundred feet to the 6,374 ft summit. A lingering snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July — either kick steps straight up it or skirt left on the rockier tread; both options rejoin near the top.
descent: Descent is a straightforward walk/scramble reversal of the ascent line — no rappelling and no technical descent gear needed. From the Plummer Peak summit, downclimb the same class 2-3 scramble terrain back to the tarn/shelf below, staying alert on the loose rock and thin tread (most parties find the down-scramble more exposed-feeling than the ascent since you're facing outward on the steeper north slope). Rejoin the boot path back to Pinnacle Saddle, then drop onto the maintained Pinnacle Peak Trail and follow its switchbacks down through the talus/heather slopes and back into forest to the Reflection Lakes trailhead. The same hazards apply in reverse: lingering snow on the steep north-facing switchbacks just below the saddle is the most common problem spot (an ice axe or trekking poles with caution are worth carrying into July in high-snow years), and the talus sections can be slick when wet. No water past the seasonal creek around 0.6 mi from the trailhead, so plan accordingly on the way down.
hazards: Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on the exposed ridge and saddle, with no shelter above treeline
Lingering snowfield on the boot path and near the saddle well into summer, icy in early morning
Steep, eroded, loose tread and exposed traverse sections on the upper Pinnacle Peak Trail switchbacks near the saddle
Winter avalanche terrain on the peak's slopes - a backcountry skier died in an avalanche near Plummer Peak in 1988

waysIn.name: Pinnacle Saddle, the tarn shelf and the north slopes
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; a snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road. The signed Pinnacle Peak Trail leaves the south side of the road, directly across from the largest of the lakes.

The trail climbs moderately through mountain hemlock and Alaska yellow cedar for the first half-mile; around 0.5 mile you get a first partial view of Rainier, and at about 0.6 mile you cross a seasonal cascading creek — the only reliable water on the hike, and dry by late summer in a low-snow year. By 0.7 mile it breaks into open talus and heather below Pinnacle's cliffs and steepens noticeably. Lingering snow on these shaded north-facing switchbacks is the trail's main hazard, since a slip on hard morning snow above the talus can slide a hiker into rock. Around 0.9-1.0 mile the trail passes beneath the cliff bands on Pinnacle's north face, then switchbacks up a short exposed final pitch to Pinnacle Saddle at about 1.25-1.3 miles and roughly 5,920-5,960 ft.

The saddle is the trail's official end and the junction where unmaintained paths fork east toward Pinnacle and The Castle and west toward Plummer and Denman.

Stevens Canyon Road is open roughly late May through late October and the small trailhead lot commonly fills by mid-morning on summer weekends.
hazards: Lingering snowfield on the steep shaded switchbacks below the saddle, icy in early morning — the most common problem spot
Steep, eroded, loose tread and exposed traverse sections on the upper approach trail
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on an exposed ridge and saddle with no shelter above treeline
Loose rock and thin tread on the final scramble, which feels more exposed descending
Winter avalanche terrain on the peak's slopes
No water past the seasonal creek low on the trail

name: Point Success via Success Cleaver
approach: From the Longmire Wilderness Information Center (2,762 ft), pick up the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles in, after climbing out of Longmire, the trail drops steeply (~400+ ft) to a log-bridge crossing of Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically damaged or washed out by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier, so check current status at the Longmire WIC before you leave, since a failed crossing can force a long reroute. Beyond the creek the trail climbs by switchbacks through old-growth forest, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek, and traverses a ridge past Devil's Dream backcountry camp (~5 mi, reliable water) before breaking out of the trees into the subalpine meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 mi and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin and open views of the Tahoma/South Tahoma icefall. From Indian Henry's, leave the maintained Wonderland Trail and follow the Mirror Lakes spur/climbers' path (several plank crossings over marshy meadow, then end of maintained tread), continuing cross-country onto the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak between about 6,000 and 6,300 ft to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. Running water is often available here from snowmelt puddles into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at ~6,300 ft (with running water nearby) is another common first-night camp for a 2-day ascent. From Point 6631, drop briefly NNE to a saddle at about 6,400 ft — the start of Success Cleaver proper. Many parties place a second high camp on the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft (snow platforms can be dug in), from which the route continues up the crest — including a knife-edge section that requires real scrambling once snow melts off it — before angling climber's-right up snow gullies that merge onto the Kautz Cleaver around 12,200–12,600 ft, then up steepening snow/ice (to roughly 45°, with an isolated ~15 ft step near 55° used to bypass a cliff band in some seasons) to Point Success at 14,158 ft. All-in this is roughly 12–13 miles and 11,500 ft of gain from Longmire to Point Success, so most parties split it over 2 days with an intermediate camp rather than going car-to-car in a single push.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than continuing on to Columbia Crest and taking the more heavily-trafficked Disappointment Cleaver off the mountain (a carry-over option some parties choose, but it requires crossing the summit crater and arranging a shuttle back to Longmire from Paradise). Down-climb the snow/ice below Point Success back onto the Kautz Cleaver chutes near 12,200–12,600 ft, then drop onto the Success Cleaver crest and retrace the loose, scree-and-choss cleaver back down to the 6,400 ft saddle by Point 6631. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no fixed rappel anchors or established rappel stations documented for this line: Success Cleaver is one of only two Rainier routes with no significant glacier travel, and it's descended on foot (ice axe, and crampons in icy years for the upper snow/ice step) rather than by rope, so the rappel count is 0. Main descent hazards are rockfall and underfoot looseness on the cleaver (worse below other parties, and worse late-season as snow recedes and exposes choss), plus sun-softened snow in the gullies by mid-morning — parties who carry over report the Disappointment Cleaver snowfield turning 'amazingly sloppy' by 10 a.m., and the same afternoon softening affects the Success/Kautz Cleaver snow, so plan an early start and be off the steep snow before it goes punchy. From Point 6631/the Pyramid Peak saddle, retrace the cross-country line to Indian Henry's Hunting Ground, then follow the Wonderland Trail back through Devil's Dream, back across the Kautz Creek log bridge (check crossing status again), and down to Longmire.
hazards: Rockfall and icefall in the three chutes climbers cross to reach the Success Glacier headwall and the Kautz Cleaver junction (~12,600 ft) — worst once the sun warms the upper mountain
Loose, unconsolidated scree and choss on the lower Divide/cleaver once snow melts out (mid-to-late summer)
Low 5th-class rock band on the final headwall below the summit plateau — exposed, sometimes wet or icy
Long, remote, lightly-traveled approach with real route-finding difficulty beyond Indian Henry's Hunting Ground (no maintained trail, sparse cairning, easy to miss the correct descent gully)
No cell coverage and no fixed rescue infrastructure on this side of the mountain — self-rescue capability required

waysIn.name: Longmire, the Wonderland Trail and Indian Henry's Hunting Ground
waysIn.season: May through September; the lower cleaver is best while it still holds snow, since it becomes loose scree once bare
waysIn.notes:
Longmire (2,762 ft) is the start, on the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles out the trail drops steeply to cross Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically wrecked by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier. Ask at the Longmire wilderness desk before you leave, because a failed crossing means a long reroute rather than a wet foot.

Beyond Kautz Creek the trail switchbacks through old growth, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek and passes Devil's Dream camp (about 5 miles, reliable water) before opening into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 miles and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin.

At Indian Henry's leave the Wonderland for the Mirror Lakes spur — plank walkways over marshy meadow, then the end of maintained tread. The path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak. From there it is cross-country on the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak, between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to Point 6631 just north of the peak. Snowmelt water is often available here into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at about 6,300 ft is a common first night.

This is one of only two routes on Rainier that avoids significant glacier travel, which is its whole appeal; the cost is that it is long, loose and unfrequented, with about 12–13 miles and roughly 11,500 ft of gain to Point Success. Most parties take two days, often with a second camp dug into the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft.
hazards: Kautz Creek crossing periodically washed out by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier; a failure forces a long reroute
Rockfall from parties above on the loose lower cleaver
Sustained loose scree and choss with no established line and sparse cairns
Knife-edge crest section, exposed once the snow melts off
Rockfall and icefall in the chutes crossed to reach the Kautz Cleaver junction, worst once the sun warms the mountain
Steepening snow and ice to roughly 45 degrees near the top; sun-softened snow by mid-morning
Very long approach with no bail-out; no cell coverage or fixed rescue on this side

waysIn.name: Kautz Creek Trail to Indian Henry's
waysIn.notes: From the Kautz Creek trailhead on the Longmire-Paradise road, follow Kautz Creek about a mile to a log-bridge crossing, then climb steeply through old growth and along the flank of Mount Ararat into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground, about 5.75 miles and 3,000 ft. Shorter than the Longmire route but uphill nearly the whole way; from Indian Henry's the climb continues as from Longmire. The Kautz Creek crossing is periodically damaged by debris flows, so ask about its status before you go.
hazards: Kautz Creek log-bridge crossing is periodically damaged by debris flows; ask about its status before going
Steep climb through old growth, about 5.75 miles and 3,000 ft to Indian Henry's
Rockfall from parties above on the loose lower cleaver
Sustained loose scree and choss with no established line and sparse cairns
Knife-edge crest section, exposed once the snow melts off
Rockfall and icefall in the chutes crossed to reach the Kautz Cleaver junction, worst once the sun warms the mountain
Steepening snow and ice near the top; no cell coverage or fixed rescue on this side
waysIn.whyThisWay: A shorter but steeper way to Indian Henry's than Longmire; the creek crossing is often damaged, and the trail has been reported closed there, so ask about it first.

name: Poltergeist Pinnacle
approach: Drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east from Glacier about 12.5 miles and turn left onto the Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), following it about 5 miles to the trailhead at its end; a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Hike the Hannegan Pass Trail about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, drop into the Chilliwack River valley and cross the river, then climb onto Easy Ridge and follow its long, partly brushy climbers' path east. Cross the Imperfect Impasse, a moat-and-cliff notch that often needs a short low fifth-class downclimb, and climb snowfields to camp at Perfect Pass, roughly 16 miles and a full day from the car. From Perfect Pass, rope up, traverse around the Challenger Arm and cross about three miles of the crevassed Challenger Glacier to the base of the pinnacle. This is a genuine multi-day glacier expedition into one of the most remote, weather-exposed corners of the North Cascades, with essentially no bailout options once committed.
descent: From the top of the technical climbing, simul-climb or belay short sections along the ridge crest (mostly low 5th class, up to 5.7) northward to Mount Challenger's main summit. From the true summit, descend the standard north-side Challenger Glacier route — the same line used for the peak's normal ascent — back down to Perfect Pass camp. Roped glacier travel is required; watch for crevasses, particularly late season as snow bridges deteriorate.
hazards: Underprotected 5.9+ R crux pitch with groundfall potential
Crevassed glacier travel required for the approach beyond Perfect Pass
Icefall hazard near Challenger Arm/Luna Cirque

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge, Perfect Pass and the Challenger Glacier
waysIn.season: Mid-July through early September, once the glacier has consolidated enough to cross and before autumn storms return. The first week of August is statistically the driest stretch here. Early-season attempts find more snow on the glacier and on the connecting ridge.
waysIn.notes: A multi-day expedition into one of the range's most remote corners with essentially no bail options once committed. From the trailhead at the end of the forest road, the trail climbs steadily through forest to Hannegan Pass, where the maintained tread ends. Drop east into the Chilliwack River valley — the last reliable water for a while — then regain height onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the remains of an old lookout on the ridge high point. From Easy Ridge, contour toward the east flank of the neighbouring peak to the notorious moat-and-cliff notch that cuts the ridge; it often still holds snow well into summer and typically needs a short stretch of low fifth-class downclimbing, or a scramble around or under a snow tunnel, to cross. Beyond it, climb snowfields to Perfect Pass, the standard base camp; whiteout here is a genuine hazard, and parties have set off toward the wrong wall. From Perfect Pass, rope up and traverse east around the Challenger Arm and cross several miles of upper glacier toward the cirque below the south side of the subsidiary summits. In lower-snow years a broken icefall blocks the direct line and most parties detour high above the first crevasse band, or drop back toward the arm for a lower line.
hazards: a severely runout crux pitch with roughly forty feet of essentially unprotectable climbing and groundfall potential
crevassed glacier travel for several miles each way, worse late season and in low-snow years
loose rock and exposed downclimbing at the moat-and-cliff notch on Easy Ridge
icefall hazard near the Challenger Arm and the cirque below
extreme remoteness, with no realistic prospect of quick outside help

name: East Face
approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FR 32, ~3,100 ft) on Trail #674. Climb steadily through forest for about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass (5,050 ft), then descend the climbers' path toward the Chilliwack River/Boundary Camp area (last reliable water for a while) before regaining elevation onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the old fire-lookout foundation/antenna remains atop Easy Peak. From Easy Ridge, contour toward Whatcom Peak's east flank to the infamous 'Imperfect Impasse' — a moat/cliff notch that often still holds snow well into summer and typically requires a short stretch of low 5th-class downclimbing or a scramble around/under a snow tunnel to cross; rope up if it looks insecure. Beyond the Impasse, climb snowfields (fog/whiteout is a real hazard here — parties have mistakenly headed for Whatcom's summit wall instead of the pass) up to Perfect Pass (~6,200 ft), the standard base camp below Whatcom Peak. Trailhead to camp is roughly 16 miles one-way with about 7,000 ft of cumulative gain — a full, long day (8-12+ hours) for a fast party, and worth splitting into two days for most. From Perfect Pass, the second-day approach crosses onto the Challenger Glacier: rope up for crevasse hazard, traverse east around Challenger Arm, and cross roughly 2.5-3 miles of upper glacier into Luna Cirque below the east side of Mt. Challenger's subsidiary summits. In lower-snow years a broken icefall blocks the direct line beneath Challenger's sub-peaks; most parties detour high above the first crevasse band (or backtrack to Challenger Arm for a lower line) to reach the base of Poltergeist Pinnacle's distinctive dike-streaked granite shield, the southernmost sub-summit between Challenger and Crooked Thumb.
descent: From the top of the route's ridge pitch, continue simulclimbing or belaying easy 5th-class terrain along the connecting ridge crest to the true summit of Mt. Challenger. This ridge traverse, not a rappel down the face just climbed, is the standard way off Poltergeist Pinnacle. From Challenger's summit, descend the mountain's standard Challenger Glacier route: downclimb or make one rappel down the short summit rock step (a compact, well-protected 5.5-5.6 wall) from fixed slings at the top. Reports differ on the rope this needs, from a 30 m rope being just enough to a 40 m rope with a few feet to spare, so carry 40 m. From the base of that rappel, rope up for glacier travel and descend the Challenger Glacier (crevasse hazard, worse late-season or in low-snow years), retracing the approach around Challenger Arm back toward Perfect Pass or a Luna Cirque camp.
hazards: severe runout / sparse protection on the 5.9+ crux pitch (R-rated)
crevasses on approach
extreme remoteness

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge, Perfect Pass and the Challenger Glacier
waysIn.season: Mid-July through early September, once the glacier crevasses are more consolidated and the pass approach is snow-free enough to travel. Earlier attempts find more snow on the glacier, on the route and on the connecting ridge.
waysIn.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the forest road, the trail climbs steadily through forest for about four miles to Hannegan Pass, where the maintained tread ends. Descend the climbers' path east toward the Chilliwack River and Boundary Camp area, the last reliable water for a while, then regain height onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the old lookout foundation and antenna remains on the ridge high point. From Easy Ridge, contour toward the east flank of the neighbouring peak to the moat-and-cliff notch that cuts the ridge; it often holds snow into summer and usually needs a short stretch of low fifth-class downclimbing or a scramble around or under a snow tunnel, and it is the cross-country crux of the approach and a common turnaround point in poor conditions. Beyond it, climb snowfields to Perfect Pass, the standard base camp; fog here is a real hazard and parties have mistakenly set off toward the wrong wall. On the second day, rope up at the Challenger Arm and cross roughly three miles of upper glacier into the cirque below the south side of the subsidiary summits, detouring high above the first crevasse band in low-snow years when the icefall blocks the direct line.
hazards: sparse protection on the crux pitch, with roughly forty feet of essentially unprotectable dike climbing off the bergschrund
crevasses on several miles of glacier approach each way
extreme remoteness with no quick outside help
the moat-and-cliff notch on Easy Ridge, wet and slippery above a deep gorge
a descent that is not back down the face — it continues over the connecting ridge and off the neighbouring summit's glacier, so glacier gear has to be carried over the top

name: South Ridge / McAllister Glacier
approach: Trailhead is the Eldorado Creek climbers' trailhead on Cascade River Road, roughly mile 20 out of Marblemount, at about 2,100 ft. From the parking pullout, backtrack a short distance downstream along the road to find a log or braided crossing of the North Fork Cascade River; ford/cross and pick up the unsigned but well-trodden climbers' path on the far bank, angling up through heavy timber. This boot path is steep and root-laced, gaining roughly 1,800-1,900 ft through forest before breaking out at a boulder field around 4,000 ft; follow cairns and the intermittent trail on the right side of the talus (roughly 1,000 vertical ft of boulder-hopping) up into the open meadows of Eldorado Creek/Eldorado Basin. From the basin, continue up benches toward the toe of the Eldorado Glacier (often called Eldorado Camp, ~6,000-7,500 ft) - this is a reasonable first-night camp and the last reliable running water before the ice cap. Rope up here: the Eldorado Glacier is broken and thinly bridged in a normal-to-low snow year, and parties have needed to weave crevasse mazes even on the standard line. From upper Eldorado Glacier, traverse north below Eldorado's east ridge and continue on the Inspiration Glacier toward Klawatti Col (~7,800 ft) - this leg is long, exposed to whiteout (several parties describe navigating the Inspiration's crevasse fields with zero visibility), and is the standard second camp for the Eldorado Ice Cap traverse that accesses Primus. From Klawatti Col camp, the climb of Primus itself is a summit-day push: down-climb or make a short (~50 ft) rappel through the notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the Klawatti Glacier. Rope up, traverse north and then east below the south side of Austera's east ridge, descending to round the end of that ridge near 6,800 ft onto the North Klawatti Glacier, and cross it (probing for hidden crevasses - this section has caught parties by surprise even in good visibility) to the foot of Primus's south face. Unrope and climb snow ramps and then talus up the face, moving right onto the south ridge for the last couple of hundred feet to the 8,508 ft summit. The trailhead sits about 6,400 ft below the summit, and the round trip takes two to three days or more; mid-to-late summer (glacier bridges more consolidated, less whiteout risk) is the recommended window.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down-climb the summit talus back to the North Klawatti Glacier, rope back up, and re-cross the glacier (same crevasse-probing caution as the approach) to the base of the McAllister-Klawatti notch. Regaining the notch back up to Klawatti Col camp is normally a climb/scramble rather than a rappel; the technical crux of the day - the short ~50 ft step between the notch and the glacier - is the one spot parties commonly fix a hand line or short rappel on the way down from the ridge, then climb the same step (with a boost from a partner or a fixed line) on the return leg. Primus's west-ridge line has a similar ~8,200 ft notch requiring a roughly 50 ft rappel to regain the glacier when descending, which lines up with an account of a party rappelling at the McAllister-Klawatti col - treat this as a single, short technical rappel rather than a multi-pitch rap descent. A single 30-60m rope is more than sufficient (a doubled 30m or single 60m easily covers 50-60 ft); anchors are natural (slings on horns/blocks) rather than bolted, since this is remote glaciated terrain with no fixed hardware. From Klawatti Col camp, the multi-day exit reverses the approach: back across the Inspiration Glacier (whiteout and crevasse hazard again), down the Eldorado Glacier, through Eldorado Basin, down the boulder field and timber climbers' path, and back across the North Fork Cascade River to the trailhead. Watch for softening glacier bridges and increased rockfall/scree looseness on the boulder-field descent in the afternoon heat.
hazards: Heavily crevassed North Klawatti/McAllister Glacier, especially late in the season
Thin, unreliable snow bridges by August-September — probe before committing weight
Very remote — long multi-day glacier approach with no cell coverage
Complex glacier routefinding around Klawatti Col in poor visibility

waysIn.name: The far end of the Eldorado ice cap: five glaciers and a notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col
waysIn.season: Mid-July through August, when the glacier bridges are most consolidated and whiteout risk is lowest
waysIn.notes:
This is the way to Primus's south side, and it comes from the opposite side of the mountain to the Thunder Creek approach. From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, cross the North Fork Cascade River, climb the steep root-laced boot path through timber, cross the boulder field around 4,000 ft following cairns on the right side of the talus, and reach the meadows of Eldorado Basin. Continue to the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and rope up — it is broken and thinly bridged in a normal-to-low snow year.

From the upper Eldorado Glacier, traverse north below Eldorado's east ridge and continue on the Inspiration Glacier toward Klawatti Col near 7,800 ft. Parties describe crossing the Inspiration's crevasse fields with zero visibility, so plan for it.

Summit day from a Klawatti Col camp: downclimb or make a short rappel of about 50 ft through the notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the Klawatti Glacier, rope up, and traverse below the south side of Austera's east ridge, rounding its end near 6,800 ft onto the North Klawatti Glacier — probing, because this stretch has caught parties by surprise even in good visibility — to the foot of Primus's south side. Then unrope and walk.

The route crosses the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister, Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers in sequence; Austera Towers is passed and bypassed on a short scree ramp along the glacier's eastern edge.
hazards: A heavily crevassed North Klawatti and McAllister glacier system, especially late season
Thin, unreliable snow bridges by August and September — probe before committing weight
Complex glacier route-finding around Klawatti Col in poor visibility
A short technical step at the McAllister-Klawatti notch that has to be reversed at the end of the day
Extreme remoteness: a multi-day approach with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Thunder Creek and the Borealis Glacier: the east ridge from Lucky Pass
waysIn.notes:
The other way onto Primus comes from the north, and it finishes on a different line: the east ridge, not this route's south side. From Colonial Creek Campground on the North Cascades Highway, walk the Thunder Creek Trail about six miles to McAllister Camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek there has washed out, so expect to ford cold, fast water or hunt for a log crossing.

Across the creek, a faint, steep boot path climbs the long, brushy lower north ridge of Tricouni Peak to the toe of the Borealis Glacier near 6,000 ft, where there is good camping. From camp, climb the glacier along its eastern edge, keeping clear of the icefall in its middle, to Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and Tricouni near 7,200 ft, and follow the east ridge to the summit on class 3 ground.

The brush on the ridge above Thunder Creek is slow going in either direction, and worse carrying skis or a long pack.
hazards: An unbridged ford of Thunder Creek at McAllister Camp
A steep, brushy boot path that is easy to lose on the ridge above Thunder Creek
An icefall in the middle of the Borealis Glacier that has to be skirted
Class 3 ground on the east ridge above Lucky Pass
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want a shorter two-day trip with fewer glaciers and fewer people; it costs a cold Thunder Creek crossing and brush, and it finishes on the east ridge, not this south side.

name: Der Sportsman
approach: Long approach into the Core Enchantments via Aasgard Pass: from the Stuart Lake Trailhead, follow the Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A junction, cross Mountaineer Creek, and switchback up to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft gain). From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining roughly 2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt, the approach's physical crux, hazardous under lingering snow (a hidden creek/moat under the talus) into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season. From the 7,841-ft pass, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn, where parties commonly bivy roughly 20 minutes from the base of Prusik's south face (there is no maintained trail for this last stretch — it's cross-country over slabs and talus). Total is roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,500+ ft one-way. Overnight camping in the Core Zone requires an Enchantments permit; the Snow Lakes Trail is a longer (9+ mile) alternative when the Stuart/Colchuck trailhead or Aasgard Pass is closed.
descent: From the summit, rappel the north side on four single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, then downclimb 3rd-class ground; one or two optional rappels right of the gully replace the downclimb. Anchors mix a bolted station near the top of pitch 1 with gear/piton anchors and slung natural features lower down — carry extra webbing to back up older tat. After the fifth rappel, scramble down to the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge and make one additional single rappel to reach easier ground before walking back to the south-face base.
hazards: sustained hard crack climbing
exposure
afternoon thunderstorms
long Enchantments approach

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the route is a hard rock climb and wants dry, warm granite
waysIn.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: steep loose scree, with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow and a fatal history
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus in the Core
5.11+ crux on the first pitch, sustained hard crack climbing far above gear
Loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side: one bolted station, then gear and slung naturals; carry webbing to back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms; Core Zone camping needs a permit

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
waysIn.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet. It is also the fallback when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed. From Lake Viviane, go up and right toward Temple Lake and then up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.
hazards: Long approach of about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain via the Snow Lakes trail to Lake Viviane
Unmarked cross-country travel past the upper lakes to the base of the south face
5.11+ crux on the first pitch, sustained hard crack climbing far above gear
Loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side: one bolted station, then gear and slung naturals; carry webbing to back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms; Core Zone camping needs a permit
waysIn.whyThisWay: Chosen to avoid the loose scree grind of Aasgard Pass; the Snow Lakes trail is longer but gentler and shaded on hot days, and it makes an easy walk out.

name: Solid Gold
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) at the end of FS Road 7601, follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) junction. Turn left, cross Mountaineer Creek (a rock-hop/log crossing and the last reliable, easy water source for a while), and switchback up 1.6 miles through forest to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) — roughly 4.1 miles and 2,000 ft from the car. Boulder-hop along the lake's east shore to the boulder field at its south end (about 5.5 miles in, 2,500 ft gained), then pick up the climbers' trail/talus leading to the base of Aasgard Pass. Aasgard Pass itself gains about 2,000 ft in only 1.25 miles of steep, loose dirt and scree — physically the crux of the approach. It's cairned when snow-free, but in early season (often into July) snow can bridge a hidden creek/moat on the left side of the gully that has caused serious injuries and at least one fatality when climbers post-holed or glissaded into it; the slope is also avalanche-prone with a spring/early-summer snowpack. From the top of the pass (7,841 ft) descend gently into the upper Core basin past Isolation/Tranquil Lake, then continue cross-country roughly 1–1.5 miles north over granite slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn (~7,400 ft); Prusik's south face and the Solid Gold start are about 15–20 minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp. Total is roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600 ft one-way from the trailhead. Overnight camping in the Core Zone requires an Enchantments lottery/walk-up permit, so many parties either link the whole climb car-to-car in a long day or secure a permit to camp at Gnome Tarn. When the Stuart Lake/Colchuck approach or Aasgard Pass is closed (wildfire, avalanche danger), the Snow Lakes Trail is a much longer (9+ miles one-way) but lower-angle alternative that eventually requires cross-country travel past Lake Viviane to reach the same south-face base.
descent: From the top of Solid Gold, most parties continue to easy ground and locate the shared 'Solid Gold' rap anchors (also used to descend Sail Away and other nearby lines) on the north side of the ridge. The standard descent is a single, full-length rappel — a 60m rope is typical — down the north face, landing on easier ground below; from there it's about a 30-minute scramble/downclimb east back around to the notch below the West Ridge and the base of the south face. Some parties instead break this into two shorter rappels from the same general anchor area depending on rope length and party size/gear drag. Anchors are natural (slung blocks/chockstones with webbing/tat), not bolted, and the anchors in this immediate area (shared with the West Ridge descent) have been periodically rebuilt and relocated as old tat accumulates — inspect and back up any station that looks worn.
hazards: sustained 5.11 climbing
serious exposure on the steep face
afternoon thunderstorms
rope management on steep rappels

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the left flank of the south face
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
As for the rest of the face: Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, left and across Mountaineer Creek — a rock-hop or log crossing, and the last easy water for a while — then 1.6 miles of switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose dirt and scree, cairned when snow-free. In early season, and often into July, snow bridges a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; people have been badly hurt and killed there postholing or glissading into it.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, drop into the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake and continue cross-country a mile or so north over slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. The start is fifteen to twenty minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Cross-country navigation over slabs with no tread for the last mile
Sustained 5.11 climbing and serious exposure on the steep face
Loose rock past the chimney at mid-height
Natural, non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side shared with several routes; inspect and back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms; Core Zone camping needs a permit

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
waysIn.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.
hazards: Long approach: about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain on the Snow Lakes trail to Lake Viviane
Cross-country travel past the upper lakes to the base of the south face
Sustained 5.11 climbing and serious exposure on the steep face
Loose rock past the chimney at mid-height
Natural, non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side shared with several routes; inspect and back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want to skip the loose, steep scree of Aasgard Pass, or the day is hot and you prefer a shaded, gentler grade, accepting a longer walk and more gain.

name: South Face (Burgner-Stanley)
approach: Long approach into the Core Enchantments via Aasgard Pass: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek and switchbacking to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft). From the south-end boulder field, ascend Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles, roughly 2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt, the approach's crux, hazardous under lingering snow into early July (hidden creek/moat beneath the talus) and avalanche-prone in shoulder season.
