From the pass (7,841 ft), travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, then contour below Prusik to the base of the south face and the start of the route — about 7.5–8 miles and 4,600 ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country travel over slabs and talus for the final stretch. Overnight camping in the Core requires an Enchantments permit; a longer Snow Lakes Trail alternative exists when Aasgard Pass or the Stuart/Colchuck trailhead is closed.
descent: Walk east from the summit and begin the north-face rappel line on slung belay stations — natural anchors (blocks/chockstones with webbing/tat); there's little to no fixed gear at the top. Plan on four single-rope rappels of about 25-30 m, then a 3rd-class downclimb; one or two optional rappels right of the gully replace the downclimb. Figure roughly an hour from the summit back to the base if the rap line isn't backed up with other parties, which does happen since several south-face routes share this descent. Bring extra tat to back up aged webbing on the natural anchors.
hazards: sustained crack climbing
exposure
afternoon thunderstorms
long Enchantments approach

The Aasgard Pass approach is loose scree/talus gaining roughly 2000ft in under a mile; the descent rappels use climber-built slung anchors rather than fixed/bolted stations, so bring cordage to build or back these up

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: terrain to climber's right cliffs out, loose rock, fatalities on record
Hidden creek beneath the talus on the pass under early-season snow
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country slab and talus travel from Gnome Tarn to the base
Loose rock near the chockstone tunnel and runout sections on the upper flare and chimney pitches
North-side rappels on climber-built slung anchors; bring cordage; the line backs up when busy
Afternoon thunderstorms and party traffic on a very popular line

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
waysIn.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet. It is also the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed. Some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.
hazards: Long approach: about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain on the Snow Lakes trail to Lake Viviane
Faint, easily lost path over granite up to Gnome Tarn and the base
Loose rock near the chockstone tunnel and runout sections on the upper flare and chimney pitches
North-side rappels on climber-built slung anchors; bring cordage; the line backs up when busy
Afternoon thunderstorms and party traffic on a very popular line
waysIn.whyThisWay: When Aasgard Pass or the Stuart Lake trailhead is unavailable, or to avoid the loose headwall for a gentler grade, at the cost of a longer walk and more gain.

name: West Ridge
approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Trail #1599) at the end of Eightmile Road/FS-7601, elev. ~3,400-3,600 ft. Hike the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed junction with the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599 continues to Stuart Lake; branch left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail). This spur crosses Mountaineer Creek on a footbridge/logs (last reliable, easy water before the basin) and then climbs a rocky, switchbacking 1.6 miles through forest and boulder fields to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft (roughly 4.1 miles and ~2,200 ft from the trailhead) - a good rest, filter-water, and gear-sort stop. Skirt the east/south shore of Colchuck Lake on climbers' trail to the large boulder field at its south end, then begin the Aasgard Pass climb: follow the outlet stream/drainage, staying climber's-left of the first band of cliffs, up steep heather, rock steps, and (in early season) snow. This is the approach crux - roughly 2,000-2,200 ft of gain in under a mile on what regulars describe as a 'jenga pile' of loose scree and talus with real fall-and-rockfall consequence; an ice axe (and crampons in early season/on residual snow) is worth carrying into July. Top out around 7,800 ft at the rim of the upper Enchantment Basin, then traverse/descend roughly 600-700 ft east through the basin's tarns and slabs, then climb north to Prusik Pass at the base of the West Ridge, the actual start of the climb. Total one-way approach is on the order of 9-10 miles with about 4,600 ft of net gain, typically taking strong parties 3.5-5 hours; a NW Forest/Enchantments overnight or day-use permit is required and quotas are tight, so many parties do this route car-to-car in a single very long day rather than camp.
descent: From the summit, the standard descent drops down the north side of Prusik Peak via a sequence of rappels, then traverses back to Prusik Pass to rejoin the approach line. Most parties make four rappels, then downclimb loose 3rd-class ground; one or two optional extra rappels can replace that downclimb - the first anchor is typically right at your feet on a flat spot at/near the true summit, with subsequent stations found by rappelling roughly 20-30m and looking climber's-left; anchors are fixed gear (slings/webbing 'tat' and rap rings/chains left by parties over the years, not bolted), so back them up or inspect carefully. Rappel lengths run mostly in the 25-30m range with one shorter first pitch; a single 60m rope is adequate for every station for a party of two, though a doubled 60m (30m per strand) can feel tight on the last traverse-y rappel, and parties of three often prefer a 70m rope for margin. After the last rappel, traverse west (skiers'-left) across talus back to Prusik Pass at the base of the West Ridge - this is not a walk-off from the summit itself, but the technical descent is short (well under an hour for an efficient party) and feeds directly back into the approach trail. From Prusik Pass, reverse the approach: down into the upper Enchantment Basin, back up and over the rim, then down the loose, steep Aasgard Pass gully to Colchuck Lake (use extra caution here - the scree that makes for a grueling ascent is equally unpleasant and slip-prone descending with tired legs), and out the Colchuck Lake/Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead. In late September and mid-October, parties made five rappels down the north side rather than four; the stations were easy to find, one worn station can be skipped for a newer one a few feet to the side, and loose rock above the lower raps is a real hazard.
hazards: Afternoon thunderstorms with limited retreat high on the ridge
Rockfall from parties climbing above on this popular line
Early-season snow/ice on approach ledges

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass to the Core, dry conditions
waysIn.season: late Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is bare talus
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the signed junction, and about four miles and 2,200 ft to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Filter here; there is nothing simple above until the Core.

Skirt the east and south shore to the boulder field at the lake's south end and start up Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under a mile, on what regulars fairly describe as a jenga pile. Follow the outlet drainage and stay climber's left (east) of the first band of cliffs. Veering climber's right toward the waterfall complex on Colchuck Peak's flank is the classic and repeatedly fatal error here — people have died on that side and it cliffs out easily. Near the top the path passes in front of a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much larger one; missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Cairns are everywhere on Aasgard and they mark more than one line. Trust the worn tread over the cairn.

Top out around 7,800-7,841 ft, then lose 600-700 ft east through the Core's tarns and slabs, then climb north to Prusik Pass. In the Core there are a couple of places where it is easy to add distance without adding progress, but the navigation is not hard in clear weather.

Most parties do this car-to-car, and a fit team should expect a 20-21 hour day; the Enchantments overnight permit lottery is competitive enough that camping is not a plan you can rely on.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: veering climber's right toward the waterfalls cliffs out and has killed people
Loose talus and rockfall the full length of the pass, worse in afternoon heat
Misleading, multiplying cairns on the pass and in the Core
No water between Colchuck Lake and the Core tarns
Unprotected 5.7 friction slab crux and loose blocks on the lower ridge
Afternoon thunderstorms with limited retreat; rockfall from parties above
Descent is rappels, not a walk-off; very long day with the descent often in the dark

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass with snow, early season
waysIn.season: May-early Jul, while the pass holds continuous snow
waysIn.notes:
Same line, different problem. With snow on it, Aasgard is an axe-and-sometimes-crampons proposition rather than a talus grind, and it is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Early-season snow softens through the day into deep, punchy stuff that hides ice underneath, and the hidden creek running beneath the talus is a real hazard where snow bridges it. The consolidated dawn snow that makes the ascent quick is also the surface that makes an uncontrolled slide easy.

On the plus side the route-finding is simpler with the talus buried, and the Core beyond the pass travels fast on snow.

On the north side of Prusik itself, snow adds both hazard and time to the rappel descent — budget for it.
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Hidden creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges
Punchy afternoon snow concealing ice; uncontrolled slide risk on the pass, up or down
Snow on Prusik's north side lengthens and complicates the rappel descent
Early-season snow and ice on approach ledges
Unprotected 5.7 friction slab crux and loose blocks on the lower ridge
Afternoon thunderstorms with limited retreat; rockfall from parties above
waysIn.whyThisWay: Early season, May to early July, while the pass holds continuous snow; quicker than talus but needs an axe, sometimes crampons, and has avalanche and hidden-creek hazard.

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments to Prusik Pass
waysIn.notes: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead, climb past Snow Lakes and Lake Viviane to the Gnome Tarn and Prusik Pass area below the peak. More gain than Aasgard Pass but no steep snow or talus headwall.
hazards: Long approach past Snow Lakes and Lake Viviane to Gnome Tarn and Prusik Pass, with more gain than Aasgard
Unprotected 5.7 friction slab crux and loose blocks on the lower ridge
Exposed traverse before the crux
Afternoon thunderstorms with limited retreat; rockfall from parties above
Descent is rappels on tat and rings, not a walk-off
waysIn.whyThisWay: To avoid the steep, loose headwall of Aasgard Pass, or on a hot day when you want shade and a gentler grade, accepting more distance and gain.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: There is no short trailhead-to-base approach for Ptarmigan Peak — it's a deep-interior Pasayten summit reached on a multi-day backpack, and the standard approach is the same trail system used to stage a high camp near Shellrock Pass. From the Slate Pass trailhead (~6,900 ft, reached via the Hart's Pass Road/FR-5400 past the Hart's Pass Guard Station), start on the Slate Pass Trail, which drops steeply through larch stands and avalanche-lily meadows for a few miles, losing roughly 1,500 ft, to its junction with the Middle Fork Pasayten River Trail / Robinson Creek Trail (#478) at around 5,300–5,400 ft. Turn north on Trail #478 and follow the Middle Fork Pasayten valley downstream, fording several tributary creeks (can run high and be a real obstacle in early-season/high-runoff conditions); this stretch has a long-standing reputation for heavy blowdown (parties describe a thousand or so downed logs), so expect slow, log-hopping travel. Continue north to the Berk Creek junction, then climb east on the Freds Pass trail, passing Freds Lake (reliable water and a common overnight stop), over Freds Pass, and across the head of the Eureka Creek basin — parties note the tread here is faint or completely obscured by blowdown near the Eureka Creek turn, so cairns and map/GPS work are needed — to Shellrock Pass (roughly 7,400–7,500 ft). A broad half-acre bench just southwest of Shellrock Pass is the standard high camp and staging area for Ptarmigan and neighboring peaks (Lago, Carru, Osceola). From camp it's off-trail: gain the ridge crest north of camp and follow open alpine tundra and talus across the shoulder of Mount Lago to Ptarmigan's south ridge — roughly 2–3 more cross-country miles and 1,000–1,200 ft of gain, mostly class 2 over tundra and talus with some loose rock on the ridge crest. A shorter, less-traveled alternative approaches from the east via the end of Eightmile Creek Road and the Eightmile Pass–Hidden Lake Trail (~15 miles) to Ptarmigan Creek, then 2–3 miles cross-country through brush to the base — shorter on paper but rougher, brushier, and far less maintained than the Slate Pass line, which is the de facto standard.
descent: This is a walk-off/scramble descent with no rappelling anywhere on the route (rappels: 0). From the summit, reverse the south ridge and talus slopes back toward the Shellrock Pass camp bench — parties describe class 3 scrambling on the ridge near Points 8165 and 8207 with one short, avoidable class-4 step, easing to class 2 tundra and talus lower down; some parties vary the line by continuing the ridge traverse over Mount Lago before dropping to the tarn/camp rather than reversing the exact ascent line, but the character (talus/tundra ridge-walking, no technical terrain) is the same either way. From the high camp near Shellrock Pass, the multi-day walk-out simply reverses the approach trail: back across the head of Eureka Creek, over Freds Pass, down Berk Creek to the Middle Fork Pasayten River Trail (#478), south up the valley, and back up the Slate Pass Trail to the Slate Pass trailhead (about 1,500 ft of final climbing on tired legs). No ropes, anchors, or rappels are used at any point on the standard route or its variations.
hazards: Sheer, seldom-seen north face — stay on the south/southeast side and don't descend toward the north rim
Loose talus (6-12 in) and a steep waterfall drainage reported on off-route descent lines
Long brush-choked valley approaches (Eureka Creek, Berk Creek) before reaching open ridge terrain
Afternoon thunderstorms on exposed alpine ridges
Extreme remoteness — near the most isolated point in the Pasayten Wilderness, far from any road or fast rescue

waysIn.name: Shellrock Pass camp and the south side
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Ptarmigan is one of the most isolated summits in this wilderness, sitting less than a mile from the most remote point in it, and the whole difficulty is getting underneath it. From the Slate Pass road end the standard line drops through larch and avalanche-lily meadows to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, runs down-valley through a stretch with a long-standing reputation for blowdown, then climbs by Fred's Lake and over the pass at the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass. A broad bench just southwest of the pass is the standard high camp for this peak and its neighbours. From the south the mountain is a rounded, tundra-covered massif and the walking is genuinely easy; its north side is another matter entirely.
hazards: Brush-choked valley approaches and heavy blowdown, thousands of downed logs on the Middle Fork valley
Faint or obscured tread near the Eureka Creek turn
Creek fords that can run high in early season
Short exposed scrambling on the connecting ridge to the south; loose rock on the ridge crest
Sheer north face immediately off the summit; stay on the south side
Afternoon thunderstorms; extreme remoteness with no fast rescue

waysIn.name: Eightmile Creek, Eightmile Pass and the Hidden Lakes
waysIn.notes: The shortest line on the map, but it starts below 3,500 ft instead of high on the Slate Pass road. From the trailhead at the end of Eightmile Creek Road, cross Eightmile Pass and follow the trail past the Hidden Lakes to Ptarmigan Creek, northeast of the peak, then go a further two or three miles to the base. Expect a long day of trail before any climbing.
hazards: Rough, brushy cross-country of two to three miles beyond Ptarmigan Creek to reach the base
Long trail approach from below 3,500 ft with little maintenance
Loose talus and scree underfoot on the summit slopes
Sheer north face; stay on the south and southeast side
Afternoon thunderstorms; extreme remoteness with no fast rescue
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you prefer the shorter map distance from a lower trailhead and accept a long day of trail first; check whether fire closures affect the trail beyond the East Fork junction.

name: Ptarmigan Traverse
approach: The standard start is the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road out of Marblemount. A well-maintained trail switchbacks 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft); the traverse proper begins there, leaving the trail southward across heather and talus toward the Cache Glacier and the notch of Cache Col, where parties rope up. Everything beyond the pass is off-trail alpine travel. This is a point-to-point traverse: the southern exit is the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road near Darrington, so most parties set a car shuttle or arrange a pickup; an out-and-back from Cascade Pass is the common alternative when the Suiattle side is washed out.
descent: From White Rock Lakes or Itswoot Ridge area, descend steeply through gullies and snowfields over Dana Glacier toward Bachelor Creek. Follow Bachelor Creek west down the canyon, navigating log-crossing sections through recovering burned forest. The maintained Downey Creek Trail eventually becomes a clear 4-5 mile path dropping 1,600+ feet through timber to the trailhead. Total descent time: 8-12 hours depending on route and conditions. Alternative: when the Suiattle River side's road or trails are washed out or closed, make it an out-and-back from Cascade Pass, heading south to White Rock Lakes and returning the same way; check current road and trail status before committing to the southern exit.
hazards: Crevasse fields on Cache Glacier and Middle Cascade Glacier are significant; early season requires careful assessment and belayed travel; late season exposes bare glacier ice and increased visual hazard
Bergschrunds at glacier heads (particularly Le Conte and Dana glaciers) require careful assessment or bypass via alternate rock routes
Avalanche danger is highest in winter/early spring and after heavy snowfall; mid-summer offers reduced but non-zero risk on south-facing slopes
Red Ledges section features narrow exposed Class 3 scrambling below Arts Knoll with 1,000+ foot exposure; loose rock and lichen hazard when wet
Route-finding complexity increases dramatically in late season when snow cover diminishes; GPS essential for backup navigation
Moats forming under cornice overhangs at high passes in mid-season; crossing requires careful assessment and may necessitate climbing cornices or detours
Loose scree and talus on slopes above ravines; rocks dislodged by one party member endanger climbers below
Afternoon thunderstorms common in July-August; electrical storm hazard requires early morning starts and descent planning

waysIn.name: Cascade Pass to Cache Col
waysIn.season: Late July to mid-September, once the Cache Glacier snow has consolidated and the cornice on the far lip of Cache Col has dropped
waysIn.notes: Drive Cascade River Road out of Marblemount to its end and take the maintained Cascade Pass Trail up its open switchbacks to the pass. That trail is the last graded tread on the whole traverse and the pass is the last easy water; everything south of it is unmarked cross-country travel over glaciers and talus. Most parties set a car shuttle to the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle side, or reverse the trip out over the pass when the southern road is washed out.
hazards: The north lip of Cache Col is commonly corniced into mid-summer and is a hazard on the way out as much as the way in
Permanent, steep snow on the Cache Glacier — axe and crampons rather than optional
No tread, no markers and no signage anywhere past the pass

name: Standard Route / Southeast Scramble
approach: From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 126.8 (about 6.5 miles east of Newhalem, on the north shoulder just east of Diablo Lake), cross the highway to the signed Pyramid Lake trailhead (roughly 1,150–1,200 ft) at the base of Pyramid Creek's cascades. The maintained, National Park Service-built tread climbs steadily through second-growth and remnant old-growth forest (some sections show past fire scarring), fords Pyramid Creek on rock/log around the 0.9-mile mark near a stand of old cedars — this is the last reliable water before the summit push, so treat it here — and continues switchbacking up to Pyramid Lake at 2.1 miles with about 1,500 ft of gain (lake sits around 2,600–2,700 ft). Pyramid Lake itself, a small deep tarn dammed by an ancient landslide, is closed to camping within a half-mile, so parties splitting the route into two days push on before making camp. Past the lake the maintained trail ends and a boot-built, cairned climbers' path takes over — tread is intermittent and easy to lose, especially in early-season snow or whiteout. At the lake's outlet, bear right (west) over a small rock knob and through a brief dip, then the path turns and climbs steeply and directly up the ridge, gaining on the order of 3,000+ ft over the next couple of miles through brush, root-pull sections, and low-grade scrambling. Partway up, look for a boulder field below a steep knob; cairns route around it via a brushy path on its south side. Above treeline the cairned path crosses slabs and heather benches past a couple of small tarns (a possible late-season water source) before the route splits: climbers bound for Pyramid continue up onto the ridge below Paul Bunyan's Stump and traverse below/around Pinnacle Peak to the saddle between Pinnacle and Pyramid, while those bound for Colonial Peak instead drop left onto a cedar bench into the Colonial Creek basin. East-facing snowfields and a notch/traverse just below the summit ridge hold snow well into summer, so carry an ice axe (crampons in early season) even in July–August. From the Pinnacle–Pyramid saddle, the final stretch to the summit is an easy, non-technical hike/scramble over talus and lingering snow patches — the summit itself is broad and nearly flat. The genuine crux of the day is route-finding above the lake: the bootpath through the boulder field, timberline benches, and the notch below the summit ridge is where parties most often go off-route.
descent: This is a full walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling anywhere on the standard route. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, downclimb back through the notch and short exposed traverse below the summit ridge (the one spot worth facing in and taking carefully, especially if icy or holding old snow), then pick back down past the false high points toward the Pinnacle–Pyramid saddle and the cairned bootpath. Below treeline, parties note the path effectively forks on the boulder-field/brush section: a 'climbers-right' line with easier, short class 3 moves is commonly used on the ascent, while a steeper, somewhat more exposed 'climbers-left' line sometimes gets taken (intentionally or by accident) on the way down — stay on cairns rather than following the first boot-track you see, since the exposed variant is not the preferred descent. In early to mid-season, the remnant snowfields on the ridge below Paul Bunyan's Stump offer glissade options for parties carrying ice axes and comfortable self-arresting; by August those slopes are mostly bare talus and it's a straightforward scramble/hike back down to Pyramid Lake, rejoining the maintained trail for the final 2.1 miles and ~1,500 ft of descent back to the SR-20 trailhead.
hazards: Loose rock and scree on the summit ridge and gully
Route-finding among several false summits along the south ridge
Steep, lingering snow on the final ~200 ft to the true summit well into summer
Brush and deadfall on the unmaintained lower climbers' trail
Afternoon thunderstorms, common in the North Cascades in summer
Sustained ~6,000 ft of gain with no reliable water source above Pyramid Lake

waysIn.name: Pyramid Lake climbers' path
waysIn.season: July to early October; east-facing snowfields and the notch below the summit ridge hold snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even in mid-season
waysIn.notes: From the small pullout on the north shoulder of the highway near milepost 126.8, cross the road to the signed trailhead at the foot of Pyramid Creek's cascades. The maintained tread climbs steadily through second-growth and remnant old-growth, fords the creek beside a stand of old cedars — the last reliable water of the day, so treat it there — and switchbacks to Pyramid Lake, where it ends. Above the lake it is a cairned boot path the whole way, intermittent and easy to lose, and the route-finding rather than the climbing is the crux.
hazards: Boot path fades completely under early-season snow or in cloud
The traverse below the peak's east-side cliffs is prone to sliding
No reliable water above the cedar ford; the timberline tarns are dry by late summer

name: Ragged Edge
approach: Same trailhead and trail as True Grit: Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine Trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway, through second-growth forest and an early creek crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish (log crossing, harder in high runoff), up through Wirtz Basin and out onto open, cairned talus, then through Headlee Pass (~4,720 ft, 2.7 mi, loose rock/rockfall exposure in the narrow couloir) and down to Vesper Creek and Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~5,000 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain) — the last dependable water. From the lake the maintained trail fades; cross the outlet and follow an obvious talus ridgeline up to the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, the small summit just northeast of Vesper. From there a slightly improbable but well-trodden heather ledge system (goat trail through it) cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft to a small notch overlooking the remnant Vesper Glacier, where the route starts. This traverse crosses steep, exposed heather that's treacherous when wet and typically holds snow into mid-to-late summer, so an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is worth carrying into early summer. Plan on 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the climb.
descent: No rappels are required — Ragged Edge tops out at or very near Vesper's summit, and the standard exit is a walk-off down the peak's east side/East Ridge back toward the Vesper-Wolf saddle, then down to Vesper Lake and out the Sunrise Mine Trail. The descent is class 2-3 scrambling/talus, occasionally holding snow into early summer (ice axe useful then), and is fast relative to the climb — most parties are back at the saddle and lake within an hour or two of topping out, with the whole car-to-car day often wrapping up in well under 12 hours. Watch for loose rock on the upper descent slopes, especially with parties above or below.
hazards: Loose rock and lichen on some belay stances (route has seen significant cleaning since the 2013 FA but caution still warranted)
Early-season snow on the saddle approach traverse

waysIn.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep; the ledge traverse holds snow into mid-summer
waysIn.notes:
Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) leaves the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 27-28 miles east of Granite Falls; about 2.3-2.5 miles of gravel end at the Sunrise Mine trailhead, around 2,400 ft, with a pit toilet and a Northwest Forest Pass requirement.

Trail #707 starts in second-growth and almost immediately crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs — a genuine obstacle in high runoff. It then climbs through Wirtz Basin and out onto open cairned talus to Headlee Pass, about 4,720 ft at 2.7 miles: a narrow rocky notch with loose footing where rockfall from parties above is a real hazard. Beyond the pass the trail drops through trees and crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, following it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 5,000 ft and 3.5 miles. That is the last dependable running water.

Stay on the ordinary Vesper summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then leave it and swing north across the slabs. Allow three hours or more from the car to the base.
hazards: Rockfall from parties above in the Headlee Pass couloir
Log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish in high runoff
Steep exposed heather on the ledge traverse — treacherous when wet
Snow on the ledge traverse into mid-to-late summer; axe worth carrying early season

name: Rampage
approach: Follow the shared Wine Spires trail: boot path down talus to Early Winters Creek, cross on a log, then climb steeply up the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the ~6,500 ft basin/camp (roughly 2 hours from the car). For Rampage, keep climbing toward Burgundy Col, then leave the trail rightward across a very loose slope onto a third-class ledge system and follow it right to its far end, where the route's corner begins. A spring near the camp bench is the last reliable water.
descent: From the top of pitch 4, parties can either scramble class-3 terrain northeast toward the base of Burgundy Spire’s North Face, downclimbing over precariously stacked blocks and flakes, to continue a link-up, or take Paisano’s standard descent: two rappels, about 30 m and 20 m, from slung horns down to the gully beneath Burgundy Col, then reverse the approach trail to the highway.
hazards: Rockfall and loose rock in the descent gully toward Burgundy Col.
Exposed, unroped-terrain scrambling if continuing to Burgundy Spire's North Face.

waysIn.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib, then the ledge system below the col
waysIn.season: Roughly late June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access ends with the highway closure
waysIn.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain rather than for the spires, and the climbers' path itself is unmarked.

Go down the talus and into the forest, cross Early Winters Creek on a log, and climb the steep timbered rib on the left, the north side, of the creek draining the col. About two hours brings you to the basin bench at roughly 6,500 ft, where there is a spring — the last reliable water.

From the bench another three-quarters of an hour or so gains the col at about 7,720 ft. Unlike its neighbour on the same pinnacle, this route wants you high, so keep going up.

The pullout is where most parties sleep. It is undeveloped and the highway is audible all night.
hazards: A very loose slope is crossed to gain the approach ledge, above the col trail
The route starts at the far right end of the ledge, not where you step onto it
Precariously stacked blocks and flakes on the scramble toward the neighbouring spire
Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water

name: Rapple Grapple
approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead, hike the Blue Lake Trail ~1.5 miles to the meadow, then take the climbers' path left past the small stream up through slabs and talus toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully. Rapple Grapple shares its first pitch with the Beckey Route, so follow the standard Beckey approach (stay right at the gully fork) to the same base.
descent: After finishing the route’s scramble and short 5.6 slab to the ridge, take the standard Liberty Bell descent, which lands close to the base of the route. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail.
hazards: Pitch 1 is shared with the popular Beckey Route — expect possible rockfall or bottlenecks from parties above at the junction.

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path, then right at the gully fork to the Beckey Route start
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the meadow, then take the climbers' path left past the small stream up through slabs and talus toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully.

Four pitches at 5.8. The route shares its first pitch with the Beckey Route, so the approach is the standard Beckey approach to the same base.
hazards: A gully fork where left and right lead to entirely different routes
Early-season snow and rockfall in the approach gully
A 5.6 boulder problem downclimbed on the descent
Queues at the shared Beckey descent rappels on busy days

name: Southeast Ridge (Crater Lake Approach)
approach: From Twisp, take Highway 20 south ~2 miles to WA-153, then south on WA-153 to County Rd 1029 (Gold Creek Loop), continuing onto County Rd 1034 (Gold Creek Road), which becomes Forest Road 4340 after about 6 miles. Turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it about 4.6 miles to the Crater Creek Trailhead (~4,750 ft; day-use fee $5, or $30/yr — Northwest Forest Pass/interagency passes accepted). Hike the Crater Creek/Crater Lakes Trail about 3.9 miles one-way, gaining roughly 2,100 ft, to Lower Crater Lake (about 6,840 ft), then continue off-trail up the southeast ridge to the ~8,000 ft col and on to the summit. In late October the spur road to the trailhead was rough but an ordinary car got through; the first stretch of the trail is shared with dirt bikes and is loose and rutted before it turns pleasant.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the boulder scramble back to the ~8,000 ft col, then descend into the Crater Lake basin. In the one documented winter ascent, the party skied this descent back to a camp at Crater Lake before skiing/hiking out the following day via the unplowed Crater Creek Road.
hazards: Avalanche terrain exists on the approach in winter/spring conditions; carry standard avalanche safety gear.
Route-finding to the ~8,000 ft col requires solid navigation skill in poor visibility, since much of the approach is off-trail.

waysIn.name: Gold Creek and the Crater Creek spur to the lake, then the south-east ridge
waysIn.season: Late July through September, once the upper ridge is out of snow
waysIn.notes:
From Twisp, run south on the highway to the Gold Creek loop and continue onto the Gold Creek road, which becomes forest road 4340 after several miles. Turn onto the Crater Creek spur and follow it a little under five miles to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft; a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs about four miles and roughly two thousand one hundred feet to Lower Crater Lake; the upper lake lies off to the south-south-west and is not on the way. From the lake the route leaves the trail and follows the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft and on to the summit.

Be careful with names when planning this one: the lake and creek names in this part of the range repeat across neighbouring drainages, and there is an unrelated lake and mountain of the same name in a different part of the state entirely. Navigate by the road numbers you turned onto and the trailhead elevation you actually parked at.
hazards: no water and no tread above the lake
loose talus and boulder-hopping along the crest
flanking gullies with very poor rock that will draw a party off the ridge
a long forest road drive on a fee trailhead
several false summits between the col and the true high point

waysIn.name: From the Libby Creek road and Trail #415, gaining the crest by the gully above the lake
waysIn.season: Late July through September, when the gully is free of snow
waysIn.notes:
The other drainage reaches the same crest. From the Libby Creek road system - a turn onto the main forest road, a left, a right onto a spur and a left onto a second spur - park at the small roadside trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft, with no toilet and no water. Trail #415 leads to the lake, past a dilapidated cabin used by some parties as a camp, with root holes and burn damage underfoot in the lower and middle miles.

This approach is shorter to the crest and pays for it with a single very loose gully, which is the crux of that side of the mountain.
hazards: a very loose gully as the only way from the lake to the crest
rockfall onto a party strung out in a confined chute
burn damage and root holes on the lower trail
no water or facilities at the trailhead
the lower peak west of the saddle, which is easiest to mistake for the summit from this side
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you prefer a shorter walk to the crest from the Libby Creek side and accept one very loose gully; wear a helmet.

name: Raven Ridge Standard Route (Libby Lake Gully-Ridge)
approach: From Twisp, drive WA-20 east a short distance to WA-153, then south on WA-153 to Libby Creek Road (County Road 1045), about 1.4 miles south of Carlton. Turn right and follow Libby Creek Road about 2.5 miles, turn left onto Forest Road 43 for about 5.1 miles, left onto Forest Road 4340 for about 1.2 miles, right onto Forest Road 4340-700 for about 1.5 miles, and left onto Forest Road 4340-750 for about 0.9 mile to the Libby Lake Trailhead (4,400–4,430 ft; roadside parking for roughly 10 vehicles, no toilet or potable water). From the trailhead, follow Libby Creek Trail #415 to Libby Lake, watching for trail damage (root holes) from the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire between roughly miles 0.8 and 2.5. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail at about 7,170 ft, used by some parties as a base camp.
descent: There is no separate descent line for the standard route — parties reverse their ascent. The crux of the descent is the loose gully: move deliberately, stay to the climber's-left (looking downhill) on more solid rock where possible, and be conscious that dislodged rock can strike other parties below. No fixed rappel anchors exist on the standard line (a rappel station has been reported on the connecting ridge toward Libby Peak/Hoodoo Peak, not on the standard Raven Ridge summit route). Retrace the trail from Libby Lake back to the Libby Lake Trailhead.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the ascent gully are the primary objective hazard and can injure parties climbing below.
A single unroped Class 4 move guards the true summit block, with real fall consequences.
The ridge crest is open and wind-exposed with little to no shelter.

waysIn.name: Libby Creek road and Trail #415 to Libby Lake
waysIn.season: Late July through September, after the snow has left the gully and before it returns to it
waysIn.notes:
From the highway south-east of Twisp, turn up the Libby Creek road and follow the forest road system - a turn onto the main forest road, then a left, then a right onto a spur, then a left onto a second spur - to the small trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft. Roadside parking takes roughly ten vehicles and there is no toilet and no water.

Trail #415 climbs from there to Libby Lake. Watch for root holes and trail damage through the burned section in the lower and middle miles, which is uneven underfoot rather than hard to follow. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail high up and is used by some parties as a base camp.
hazards: an extremely loose gully that is the defining hazard of the route
rockfall from parties above in a confined chute
burned-out trail with root holes underfoot in the lower miles
no water or facilities at the trailhead
loose talus and large boulders on the ridge traverse
a lower summit west of the saddle that is easily mistaken for the top

waysIn.name: From the Crater Creek road and the lake basin, gaining the crest from the south-east
waysIn.season: Late July through September
waysIn.notes:
The same summit is reached from the next drainage south. From the highway, take the Gold Creek road system on to forest road 4340 and then the Crater Creek spur to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft, where a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs a little under four miles to the lake, and from there the route continues off-trail up the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft.

This avoids the loose gully entirely at the price of more off-trail ridge travel, so it is the better option for a party unhappy with a confined chute and the worse one for a party short of time.
hazards: a long off-trail ridge with no tread and no water above the lake
loose talus and large boulders on the crest
flanking gullies that will pull a party off the ridge into very loose ground
a day-use fee area with a long forest road drive
intervening high points that hide the true summit
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want to avoid the loose, confined gully, or snow still lies in it, and accept more off-trail ridge travel on the south-east side.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Reynolds Creek Trailhead (~3,100–3,170 ft, reached via Forest Road 4435, which crosses the Twisp River near Mystery Campground before the Spur 4435-015 turnoff to the trailhead), the route follows Reynolds Creek Trail #402, an unmaintained, primitive Forest Service trail entering the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. Trail #402 climbs steadily through mixed conifer forest along Reynolds Creek for roughly 3 miles to the confluence where the South Fork of Reynolds Creek meets the main creek (approx. 4,800–5,000 ft) — parties describe scooting across a downed log to make this crossing, which can be a genuine ford in high early-season flow. This confluence is the last reliable, easy water source before the upper basin, so fill up here. Beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread and follow the South Fork drainage, staying roughly 50 ft above the creek to avoid the worst brush and log-hopping directly in the streambed. Expect about 2 miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber, and a boot-path/game-trail tread that comes and goes — this is the route-finding crux of the approach, and parties specifically flag the numerous fallen logs and dense brush here. The drainage opens into a broad talus/scree basin around 5,500–5,700 ft directly below Reynolds Peak's southeast face and the gully/snowfield leading to its east ridge. This basin and the gully above it hold snow well into summer in most years, so carry an ice axe (and traction in early season) even on an otherwise dry-looking late-summer day. From the basin, ascend the scree, talus, and (seasonally) snow of the SE slopes/gully to a saddle/notch on the peak's east ridge, then finish with a short, exposed class 2–3 scramble (occasionally reported as harder, class 3–4, depending on snow coverage) up sound granite summit rocks to the 8,517 ft high point. An alternate, more scenic but similarly long approach exists via Williams Creek Trail and War Creek Ridge from a different Twisp River Road trailhead, but Reynolds Creek Trail #402 is the standard, shorter line. The longer Williams Creek/War Creek Ridge alternative can be combined into a loop with Abernathy Peak or Twisp Pass, running roughly 24 miles round trip with about 8,300 ft of cumulative gain.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — there is no rappelling on the standard route. Downclimb the class 2–3 summit rocks back to the saddle/notch on the east ridge, then descend the scree, talus, and snow gully back into the SE basin at ~5,500–5,700 ft. When the gully still holds good snow (common well into summer), this section glissades or plunge-steps quickly; once it melts out to bare scree/talus later in the season it becomes a slower, loose descent — go one at a time through any group to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below. From the basin, pick up the boot path along the South Fork's climber's-right bank back to the log crossing at the South Fork/main Reynolds Creek confluence (~4,800–5,000 ft), then follow Reynolds Creek Trail #402 the remaining ~3 miles of forest trail back to the Reynolds Creek Trailhead. This is a full retrace/walk-off descent with no fixed anchors or rappel stations reported anywhere on the standard route; treat any exposed class 3 downclimbing on the summit rocks with care rather than as a rappel substitute.
hazards: Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and summit gully — explicitly flagged for this route and confirmed by old avalanche debris found in the summit gully after a January storm during a documented winter ascent
Loose rock/talus on the Class 3-4 south summit block
Deadfall and brush on the lower Reynolds Creek Trail from infrequent maintenance
Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer on this dry, east-side Cascades peak
Breakable snow crust and postholing on spring ascents/descents

waysIn.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge
waysIn.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid. It can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, and it joins the same finish as the Reynolds Creek way.
hazards: Longer day with big elevation gain via Williams Lake and over Williams Butte and War Creek Ridge
Drop through a cliff-band boulder break into the upper South Fork basin; route-finding needed
Avalanche terrain on the summit gully whenever it holds snow
Loose rock and talus on the upper gully and Class 3-4 summit block
Lingering snow in the summit gully through early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want a longer, scenic outing on good trail instead of the brushy creek bushwhack, or an overnight or loop with a neighbouring summit, camping at the lake.

waysIn.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
waysIn.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.
hazards: About two miles of intermittent bushwhack above the confluence through slide alder and downed timber, with a boot path that comes and goes
Deadfall and heavy brush on the lower unmaintained trail
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and summit gully whenever they hold snow
Loose rock and real exposure on the summit block
Breakable crust and postholing on spring ascents
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
Since the 2018 fire the lower trail is largely buried in blowdown and brush and is often lost

name: Ridge Traverse from East Fury
approach: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead and walk down to Ross Lake, where most parties take the paid water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing rather than walking the lakeshore trail. From the landing it is about 9.4 miles of nearly flat old-growth trail up the Big Beaver valley to Luna Camp, the usual first night. About a mile and a half beyond camp, leave the trail on a small boot path and cross Big Beaver Creek just north of where Access Creek comes in, around 2,460 ft. Depending on the year this is a log or a wade. Then climb the north side of Access Creek on a faint, brushy climbers' path through Access Creek basin, up the south gully and around the south side of Luna Peak to Luna Col, the usual high camp. From Luna Col, follow the ridge toward Fury over class 3 ground with many short ups and downs. Drop to traverse heather slopes on its south side to the Southeast Glacier near 6,700 ft, then climb the right side of the glacier to steeper snow and a possible bergschrund below East Fury's summit, where the traverse to the West Peak begins. Allow three to five days for the round trip. The Luna Fire closure has shut the Big Beaver Trail from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, including Luna Camp, and bars cross-country travel from the closed trail; check the park's current fire closures before planning.
descent: Descend the towers you climbed by reversing the route and setting rappels off poor-quality anchors on chossy rock. Each rappel down makes retreat progressively more difficult. Once off the traverse, descend the east side of East Fury to the saddle on loose Class 2-3 talus, then descend the Southeast Glacier back to Luna Col and the main Access Creek drainage.
hazards: Chossy, unconsolidated granite prone to failure
Limited solid anchor placements for protection or rappels
Exposure on multiple tower sections with 100+ ft drops
Poor-quality tat on descent - unreliable fixed anchors
Avalanche potential in early season on approaches

waysIn.name: Climb East Fury first; the traverse starts on its summit
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
This route has no approach of its own in the ordinary sense. It is the connecting ridge between the two summits of Mount Fury, and the only way to arrive at its start is to have climbed East Fury, which is reached from the Ross Dam Trailhead by water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, the Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col, Luna Col and the Southeast Glacier.

Budget the East Fury ascent as a full day in its own right before this one begins, and note that the traverse is about half a kilometre of ridge, which says nothing useful about how long it takes.
hazards: Reached by climbing East Fury first: crevasses, a moat/bergschrund fall site at the glacier margin, loose Class 4-5 rock
Dense brush and devil's club on the Access Creek approach
Chossy, unconsolidated granite on the towers, prone to failure
Poor-quality anchors for rappels on chossy rock; each rappel makes retreat harder
Exposure on tower sections with 100+ ft drops and scarce reliable protection
Loose Class 2-3 talus on the descent of East Fury's east side
Extreme isolation: a committing ridge between two of the most remote summits in the range

name: Rikki Tikki Tavi
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), follow the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) to Colchuck Lake — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek at 1.5 miles, turning left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the Stuart Lake Trail junction, finishing with a boulder-moraine climb to the outlet (2.5-3 hours, last reliable water). Continue around the west shore to the lake's south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; holds wet snow into July, with a real slip-and-fall history), then cut climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Rikki Tikki Tavi (5.11, 5 pitches) sits to the right of The Scoop on the wall; expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the base. Total trailhead-to-base time is around 3.5-4 hours.
descent: Rikki Tikki Tavi's five pitches top out in the upper-wall area shared with The Scoop and Milk n' Honey, and most likely shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard summit descent: class 3-4 scrambling around the right side of the true summit block down to a sandy scree/talus gully, descended clockwise back around the peak to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr), with a short step near the top sometimes eased by an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn (natural anchor) on the east side. The Scoop, immediately to its left, is noted as having natural tree/horn anchors that allow rappelling the route itself as an alternative, which may also be an option here given the shared rock character.
hazards: Exposed, unroped 4th-class summit ridge scramble to finish

name: Roan Wall - Center Stage
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
descent: Descend by rappelling the route itself, using the new double-ring stainless-steel bolted anchors present at each belay station; bring double ropes.
hazards: Creek ford can be difficult at high flow, especially early season.
Approach navigation through alder and the watercourse is not straightforward and benefits from prior beta.

waysIn.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
waysIn.season: Summer, once the ford is low; the Roan Wall base commonly holds residual avalanche snow well into the climbing season
waysIn.notes:
From Highway 530 in Darrington turn south on Madison Ave, follow it to a T, turn right on Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, and follow it to where a washout gates it off.

Walk the old roadbed. A landslide crossing comes about five minutes in and is flagged. The original road end is about 30-40 minutes from the car. Carry on along the old trail for another 20-30 minutes.

The turn-off is a landmark, not a sign: a large dry streambed roughly 50 feet wide and full of white boulders. This is the last turnoff before the Squire Creek trail swings south out of the valley toward Squire Creek Pass — if the trail starts climbing away southward, you walked past it.

Drop about 200 feet down the streambed, trending left into alders, where an informal path becomes visible. Follow that upvalley for roughly 30 minutes to a ford of Squire Creek. Past a small creek channel the trail fades; keep following the underground creek bed and it opens into the basin, about two hours from the car. Allow 3 to 3.5 hours in all to reach the base of the wall.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek — difficult in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
Residual avalanche snow at the base for much of the season
Faint informal path through alder; the trail fades entirely in the basin

name: Roan Wall - Stage Right
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
descent: From the top of Stage Right, find a narrow ledge and work left and slightly downward to reach the top of the Center Stage route. From there, rappel Center Stage's bolted double-ring anchors (the face is described as clean and open) using double ropes.
hazards: Creek ford can be difficult at high flow, especially early season.
Sustained slab climbing with friction cruxes demands careful footwork, particularly if rock is damp.

waysIn.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
waysIn.season: Summer, once the ford is low; the base commonly holds residual avalanche snow
waysIn.notes:
Darrington: Madison Ave south to a T, right on Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, to the washout gate.

Old roadbed on foot — flagged landslide crossing about five minutes in, original road end at 30-40 minutes, then 20-30 minutes more on the old trail to a large dry streambed about 50 feet across and full of white boulders. That streambed is the Waterfall Basin turn-off and it is the last one before the trail heads south for Squire Creek Pass.

Descend the bed about 200 feet, trend left into alders to pick up an informal path, follow it roughly 30 minutes to the ford of Squire Creek, then continue as the trail fades along the underground creek bed until the basin opens up, about two hours from the car.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
Residual avalanche snow at the base
Path fades in the basin

name: West Route (Rock Mountain Trail)
approach: From the Rock Mountain Trail #1587 pullout on US-2 (small dirt lot on the north side of the highway near the powerlines, no facilities), the trail launches immediately uphill on what was formerly a service road. At about 0.33 mile a signed junction marks where the route leaves the old roadbed, narrows to true single-track, and begins climbing alongside Schilling Creek — the creek runs close to the tread here but drops away and is not a reliable water source higher up, so top off early; there is essentially no accessible water for the rest of the climb. From here the trail settles into a long, relentless run of tight switchbacks (climbers count 90-plus) up an open, south/southwest-facing slope with zero shade, making this a notably hot ascent in summer. Around 1 mile a ledgy switchback opens the first real views down-valley. By roughly 2.1 miles (~5,000 ft) the grade eases as the switchbacks give way to more open hillside; at about 2.6 miles the trail passes an old (inactive) artillery-range warning sign, a quirky historical landmark, before entering heather-carpeted subalpine meadows around 2.8 miles. At roughly 3.2 miles and 6,000+ feet the trail tops out on the crest at a junction with the Nason Ridge Trail #1583 — this is the key navigational junction; go left (west) along the ridge. Around 3.7 miles the route passes the junction with the alternate Snowy Creek Trail #1531 approach (reached via Smithbrook Road #6700, a longer but more scenic drive-in), which joins from the south. Beyond this the tread thins into more of a ridge scramble path leading to a false (south) summit; use real caution on the short, narrow connecting ridge over to the true summit, which can hold a cornice or residual snow into early summer. The old lookout foundation and true summit (~6,850 ft) is reached around 3.95-4.0 miles one-way. Overall this is a Class 1-2 trail/scramble with no technical climbing when snow-free, but expect loose scree on sections of the switchbacks, essentially no shade or water above the creek crossing, and genuine route-finding/exposure caution on the false-summit-to-true-summit ridge, especially with snow present.
descent: Descend by the same line you came up — Rock Mountain's West Route is an out-and-back scramble with no rappelling involved (0 rappels). From the true summit, re-cross the narrow, sometimes corniced connecting ridge back to the false (south) summit, then drop back onto the Rock Mountain Trail #1587 tread, passing the Snowy Creek Trail #1531 junction (~3.7 mi) and the Nason Ridge Trail #1583 junction (~3.2 mi) on your way back down into the meadows and then into the long switchback section. The loose, rocky switchbacks are noticeably harder on knees and ankles heading down than they were on the way up — trekking poles help a lot here. In early season, when snow lingers on the upper switchbacks and across the false-summit ridge, microspikes are commonly recommended for the descent since the slope faces southwest and can get soft and post-holey by midday, then firm and slick in morning/evening shade. Retrace back through the ~0.33-mile junction onto the old roadbed to the trailhead.
hazards: No reliable water on route — carry 3+ liters, more in hot weather
Steep, fully exposed south-facing switchbacks with heat/sun exposure and no shade
Sharp drop-offs near the Schilling Creek crossing and along the summit ridge scramble
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge and final scramble to the true summit
Lingering snowfields on north-facing terrain (Rock Lake basin, upper ridge) into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms common July-August on this exposed ridge
Habituated mountain goats near the summit — keep distance, don't let them approach for salt
Signed artillery-range warning at mile 2.6 on Trail #1587 — stay on the established trail

waysIn.name: Trail #1587 from US-2 to the Nason Ridge crest
waysIn.season: Late June to October; snow lingers
waysIn.notes: One of the steepest maintained trails near Stevens Pass, and it starts working immediately. From the dirt pullout on the north side of the highway the tread climbs on an old service road beneath powerlines, leaves the roadbed at a signed bend about a third of a mile up, and then runs into ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade at all. Schilling Creek near the bottom is the only accessible water on the climb and it drops away quickly, so fill everything at the car and carry three litres or more. The grade eases into heather meadows around 2.8 miles and the tread tops out on the crest at about 6,000 ft.
hazards: Ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade; heat and sun load
No reliable water above the creek low down; carry 3+ liters
Loose rock and jumbled talus on the upper ridge and final scramble
North-facing snow patch below the summit ridge can persist into fall and goes slick by afternoon
Cornice or residual snow on the narrow connecting ridge into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed crest
Habituated mountain goats near the summit; keep your distance

waysIn.name: Snowy Creek trail from Smith Brook road
waysIn.notes: Drive Smith Brook road six miles and the narrow, brushy Snowy Creek road a further three and a half to a small trailhead with very limited parking. The trail follows Snowy Creek through old growth, then climbs to the crest and joins the main route about half a mile short of the summit. It is shorter and far less steep than the highway trail. The Snowy Creek road has been closed by storm damage since June 2026, so check before driving it.
hazards: Narrow, brushy Snowy Creek road is long and has been closed by storm damage; trailhead parking is very limited
Joins the main route about half a mile short of the summit; no reliable water
Loose rock and jumbled talus on the upper ridge and final scramble
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain and a cornice or residual snow on the narrow connecting ridge into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed crest
Habituated mountain goats near the summit; keep your distance
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a shorter, gentler and more scenic climb than the steep highway trail; it is north facing, so snow lingers, and the road has had storm damage, so check it is open.

name: North Face / Ruth Glacier
approach: From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FR-32, ~5.3 miles off Mt. Baker Highway/SR 542) follow Hannegan Pass Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley. The first ~2-2.5 miles climb gently through old-growth and subalpine forest with Ruth Creek running alongside and views north to Mt. Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge; a couple of informal campsites and use paths sit in this stretch. Around mile 3, at Hannegan Camp (a designated backcountry camp and the last reliably running water on the standard line), the grade kicks up into switchbacks that climb through meadows to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft) at about mile 4 — roughly 2,000 ft of gain from the car. At the pass, leave the maintained trail for a climbers'/boot path heading east then south, staying on the south side of a small pond; the tread is faint and partly hidden in trees here and is the easiest place on the whole route to lose the line, especially in flat light or early morning. Continue up and left around the base of a cliff band on a shoulder, then traverse south across heather and talus to gain the broad ridge feeding the toe of the Ruth Glacier's north slope (~6,000-6,200 ft) — rope up and get on glacier gear here. The lower glacier is a moderate, welcoming-looking snow/ice slope, but it has produced at least one documented crevasse fall in years with thin or soft cover, so treat it as glaciated terrain the entire way rather than a snow walk. Continue up and climber's-left to the broad notch just northwest of Ruth's summit (~6,600 ft); most parties camp on the far (south) side of this notch on snow to minimize impact before the final push. There is no reliable running water above Hannegan Camp/Ruth Creek in a typical snow year, so plan to melt snow or carry enough in. Round trip is roughly 12 miles and 4,000-4,200 ft of gain car-to-car; most parties split it over two days with a camp near the notch, though fit, fast parties complete it in one long day.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — the standard North Face/Ruth Glacier route has no technical rappelling; rope, axe, and crampons are carried for glacier travel, not rock protection. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the glacier's moderate north-slope snow/ice back to the ridge toe below the notch, staying roped and alert for the same crevasse hazard encountered on the way up (afternoon softening can open bridges that were solid at dawn, so an early start/turnaround is worth planning around). Pick up the climbers' path back along the shoulder, staying above/right of the cliff band, and drop past the pond south of Hannegan Pass to regain the maintained trail. From Hannegan Pass, follow Trail #674 back down its switchbacks past Hannegan Camp and out the gentle Ruth Creek valley grade to the trailhead.
hazards: Loose, sometimes muddy tread with cliff exposure on the unmaintained climbers' path between Hannegan Pass and Ruth Arm, especially the steep traverse below Point 5930
Open crevasses on the Ruth Glacier — usually small (under 10 ft) but larger/more numerous in early season or low-snow years
Afternoon warming softens snow bridges and increases postholing/wet-slide risk on the Pt. 5930 traverse
Black flies and mosquitoes can be heavy around Hannegan Pass and Ruth Arm into midsummer

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 and the climbers' path past the pond to the toe of the Ruth Glacier
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Read the name carefully. This route is filed under a name that encodes the direction you walk, not the side you climb: the line goes over Hannegan Pass and up the north-side Ruth Glacier. Its aspect is N. A party expecting south-facing slopes will be looking for the wrong mountain-side all day.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FR-32, about 5.3 miles off SR-542, follow Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley. The first 2-2.5 miles climb gently through old growth with Ruth Creek alongside and views north to Mount Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge. Around mile 3, Hannegan Camp is a designated backcountry camp and the last reliably running water on the standard line; above it the trail switchbacks through meadows to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, about mile 4 and roughly 2,000 ft of gain.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail for a climbers' path heading east then south. Most parties camp on the far side of the notch northwest of Ruth's summit, on snow, to keep impact down.
hazards: A faint climbers' path at Hannegan Pass that parties routinely lose in flat light
A glacier that looks like a snow walk and has produced a crevasse fall
No reliable running water above Hannegan Camp in a typical snow year
Route-finding around a cliff band on a shoulder with no cairns
A long valley walk out after a summit day, commonly finished tired

name: Ruth Peak Scramble
approach: From the Sol Duc Trailhead (~1,900 ft), follow the Sol Duc River Trail through old-growth forest to Sol Duc Park, then climb to Heart Lake (7.85 mi) and the High Divide/Bailey Range junction (~8.3 mi, ~5,050 ft). Leave the maintained trail here and drop off the High Divide via the boot-path known as the 'Catwalk' (class 2-3 scrambling that can hold snow into midsummer), passing below Cat Peak and Stephen Peak. Continue cross-country toward Eleven Bull Basin, a meadow on Ruth Peak's south flank with reliable water and established tent pads on the knob above the basin — roughly 15 mi and ~6,000 ft of cumulative gain from the trailhead. From camp, scramble class 2-3 talus/scree north to the summit.
descent: Downclimb the same class 2-3 slopes back to Eleven Bull Basin camp. If continuing the Bailey Range Traverse rather than exiting, note that water is scarce for roughly an hour past Eleven Bull Basin heading toward Cream Lake — top off water bottles at camp before moving on. Parties exiting the way they came reverse the Catwalk and High Divide Trail to Sol Duc Trailhead.
hazards: Off-trail navigation over talus, scree, and brush — unmarked and largely unmaintained past the High Divide/Bailey Range junction
Lingering snowfields and steep snow on the Catwalk and Ruth's north-facing slopes well into early summer
Fairchild Glacier on Ruth's NE aspect — minor crevasse hazard if approaching or traversing that side
Black bears are common through the Seven Lakes Basin/Bailey Range corridor — bear canister required
Long dry stretch (roughly an hour past Eleven Bull Basin toward Cream Lake) with no reliable water
Fast-changing Olympic weather — afternoon cloud and thunderstorm buildup can quickly degrade visibility for off-trail travel

waysIn.name: High Divide and the Catwalk to Eleven Bull Basin
waysIn.season: Late July to mid-September
waysIn.notes: Sol Duc through old growth to Heart Lake and the High Divide junction, then off the maintained trail onto the boot path called the Catwalk below Cat Peak and Stephen Peak — Class 2 to 3 with a full pack and holding snow into midsummer. Almost always climbed as a waypoint on a longer traverse.
hazards: Off-trail navigation over talus, scree and brush with no maintained tread
Snowfields on the Catwalk and on north-facing ground into early summer
Crevasse hazard on the small glacier draping the northeast aspect
A long dry stretch onward from camp with no dependable water
Fast-building afternoon cloud that ruins visibility for off-trail travel
